**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, the owner can't unilaterally change how you pay rent. Check the points below before you pay anything into the new account.

## What the law says

- **Rent payment is set by your agreement.** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified. Otherwise, it is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing the payment method requires agreement.** The provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs (including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees) you may incur with a payment method before you consent to using it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **A no-extra-cost method must be available.** A method that incurs no additional costs (other than your own bank or account fees) must be reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must also permit Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **You are entitled to a receipt.** If you pay by a method other than in person and request a receipt, it must be given within 5 business days. It must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond rules.** The provider or agent must give the bond to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (the Authority) within 10 business days after receiving it, with the completed bond lodgment form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may notify the Authority [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Until the bond is paid to the Authority, the provider holds it on trust for you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Transfers must be notified.** If a provider assigns or transfers their rights and duties under the agreement, the provider and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an owner taking over from an agent counts as a transfer in this sense.
- **Contact changes must be notified.** The provider must give you written notice of any change to their agent or contact information before the end of 7 days after the change .

## What to check or ask before paying

1. **Get the change in writing and agreed by you.** Ask for a written variation. Under the law, a change to the payment method needs your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Don't treat an agent's message as a unilateral change.
2. **Check the fees.** Ask what costs, if any, apply to the new payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Confirm the method is fee-free apart from your own bank fees, since that's the standard the law sets [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the payment method is permitted.** Ask whether the new arrangement allows Centrepay or another electronic method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm who the payee is.** Ask who owns the account and why the owner is now collecting rent. The agent's notice should identify the owner and agent contact details, and any change to those details must be notified in writing within 7 days .
5. **Confirm your bond status.** Ask for the bond lodgment form and confirm it was lodged with the Authority within 10 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check whether you have received the Authority's receipt, which should come within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If it hasn't come within 15 business days of your payment, you can contact the Authority [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The regulations list the Authority's email as rtba@justice.vic.gov.au and its phone number as 1300 137 164 .
6. **Get a receipt for each rent payment.** Request one if you don't pay in person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
7. **Confirm the bank details independently.** The documents don't cover how to verify bank account changes or protect against payment fraud. As a general precaution (not from the sources), confirm the new details by calling a number you already have for the agency or owner, not one provided in the new message.

## Limits of the documents

The documents don't say whether changing bank account details, with no change in payment method, counts as a change "by agreement" under the rent payment rules. They also don't say whether an agent-to-owner handover is a transfer that triggers the 5-day Authority notice. Ask the agent or owner to clarify these points, or seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Authority.

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents do not clearly say the app may charge a card fee. Two provisions point against it, but I can't confirm how they apply to a card fee collected by a third-party payments company.

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", dated 25 Nov 2025). Its metadata gives version "111", in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026, so it covers 15 January 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). ## What the law says

- **A fee-free method must be available.** The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a person and 400 for a body corporate (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your free bank transfer is likely to satisfy this, though the Act doesn't say whether a slower method is still "reasonably available".
- **You must be told about fees first.** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur by using a particular payment method, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic payment facility charges.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for the "establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 51(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card fee in a rent app could arguably fall within this wording, but the Act doesn't define "electronic payment facility" in the text I retrieved. That is my reading, not something the documents state.
- **Businesses other than the agent.** A person carrying on a business must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Residential rental providers, their agents, and authorised deposit-taking institutions are excluded from this rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?

It may matter, because the rules differ by who receives the fee.

- **Fee to the payments company.** Section 51A is aimed at businesses other than the provider, the agent and banks, so it could apply to a separate payments company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, it only bites on a "prescribed matter", and the regulations I retrieved don't show what is prescribed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't say whether a card fee is covered.
- **Fee to the agent.** The agent is excluded from s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The agent is still bound by s 42(4) and s 42(7). Section 51(3) applies to "a person", so it appears to cover an agent too [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Use the free bank transfer.** Section 42(4) requires a no-extra-cost method to be reasonably available, and you are not obliged to use the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the agent for the fee details in writing before you consent to card payment.** This includes who receives the fee and how much it is. Section 42(7) requires them to give you this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Query the fee with the agent.** You could cite ss 51(3) and 51A and ask them to explain why it is lawful [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form also says the provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check your agreement.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement, and you and the provider can change that by agreement (s 42(2), (6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether the card fee is lawful when a third-party payments company collects it, or what remedy you would have. For a definite answer you would need the prescribed matters under s 51A, which are not in the text I retrieved.

# Your options on 15 October 2019

I relied on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088** (file `rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf`, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019). Its metadata shows it in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Cancelling before you move in.** A tenancy agreement terminates if you haven't entered into possession and have given the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for human habitation (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You haven't moved in or stayed, which fits this section. Picking up the keys is not clearly the same as "entering into possession". The documents don't say, so that is a point to check.
- **Landlord's repair duty.** The landlord must ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition on handover.** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day. You are not required to move in if they aren't, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually enter (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This covers "vacant and reasonably clean". It doesn't mention damp, mould or rot.
- **Condition report.** If you paid a bond, the landlord must give you 2 signed copies of a condition report before you move in. You return one copy within 3 business days after entering, signed or with your endorsement agreeing or disagreeing (s 35) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition (s 36) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

**1. Cancel (s 226).** Give the landlord a notice of termination stating that the premises are not in good repair and/or are unfit for human habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved don't give a required form, notice period or any bond-refund consequence for this notice, so I can't say more on those points.

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Urgent repairs (s 72).** These include a serious roof leak and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" (s 3 definition). The in-force definition doesn't list mould, damp or rot by name [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If a repair is urgent, you must first take reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do it immediately. If you can't, you can arrange it yourself and give 14 days' written notice of the repair and its cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for an order for urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs (ss 74–76).** Give the landlord written notice. If the landlord hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you are still unsatisfied after the Director's report, you can apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the report. You can also apply without the report if you haven't received it within 90 days of applying for it (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs and set a deadline (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent.**
- **Rent Special Account (s 77).** After you have given notice requiring repairs, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. It may do so for a set period if the landlord has failed to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Compensation (s 212(5)).** If the Tribunal orders compensation in your favour, the order may take the form of a refund or reduction of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't set out the full application process for compensation.
- **Excessive rent (ss 45–47).** You can complain about excessive rent to the Director if the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or if you've received a rent-increase notice. The Tribunal considers the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither situation clearly applies to you now.

I found no provision giving an automatic right to a rent reduction for these defects before you move in.

## A note on amending text

The same document reproduces amending provisions in its endnotes, using "renter" and "residential rental provider" wording. These include a new s 91L (adding "do not meet any rental minimum standards") and mould or damp caused by the building structure being added to urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't show these were in force on 15 October 2019, so I haven't relied on them.

**Practical step:** document the damp, mould and rot now with dated photos, and put everything to the landlord or agent in writing.

## What the law says

**Entry for a smoke alarm check**
- The rental provider has a duty to ensure smoke alarms work, have batteries, and are tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entry is allowed where it is "required to enable the residential rental provider to carry out a duty under this Act" (s 86(1)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check fits this ground.
- For that ground, entry can happen between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice (s 85(b)(iii)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Seven days' notice and a 10 am–12:30 pm window are within these limits, as long as the day isn't a public holiday.
- The notice must be in writing and say why the agent wants to enter. It must be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. (s 88) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The entry must be in a reasonable manner, and the people entering must not stay longer than needed (s 87) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A renter has a duty to permit entry that follows this Division (s 89(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations' summary of renter rights says the same: the renter "must allow entry" where the rental provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be home?**
The retrieved documents don't say that a renter must be present. They also don't say what happens if you aren't there and the agent uses a key. The duty is to permit entry that follows the rules, and the rules are the notice, time and purpose requirements above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm either way from these documents whether the agent may let themselves in with a key when you're out.

**The $90 rebooking fee**
Nothing in the retrieved text authorises a fee for missing or rebooking an entry. The charge provisions I found (ss 50–51A) cover holding deposits, charges for making or renewing an agreement, charges for a prospective renter inspecting, rent-payment cards and direct debit, and application and rent payment fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). None of them mentions a rebooking fee, so the documents don't answer this directly. I can't say the fee is prohibited, but I found no basis for it.

## What you can do
- **Ask the agent in writing** which section of the Act allows the $90 fee and where it says you must be present.
- **Check the notice.** It must be in writing, state the reason, and have been posted or hand-delivered within 8 a.m.–6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Agree a different time.** Entry is also allowed "at any time agreed with the renter" if you consented within 7 days before the entry (s 85(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal.** Under s 89(2)–(3) you can apply for an order specifying or limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Complain about non-compliant entry.** If entry doesn't follow the Division, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining the rental provider and agent from entering for a set period (s 91) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering without reasonable excuse and not in accordance with the Division is also an offence (s 91A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

For a definite answer on the key and the fee, you may want to contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal service. The documents I retrieved don't resolve those two points.

# Changing from agent to owner-managed: what the law says and what to check

**Documents applied (both in force on 8 November 2022):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf"), version 101, in force 7 Sep 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf"), version 002, in force from 1 Jun 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved text gives these version numbers in the file names and metadata. It does not reproduce an "Authorised Version No." line.

---

## What the law says

**1. The owner must tell you about the change in writing.**
- If there is no agent, the owner must give you their full name, an address for service of documents, and an emergency telephone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The owner must give you written notice of any change in that information before the end of 7 days after the change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The standard lease form says the same. The owner must notify the renter within 7 days if the agent or owner details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The agent's say-so alone may not meet this requirement. Check whether you have received a written notice.

**2. Rent is paid where and how your lease says.**
- Rent is payable at the place named in the agreement. If none is named, it is payable at the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- It is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The owner and renter *may change the manner of payment by agreement* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). My reading is that you are not required to switch accounts unless you agree. The documents do not say this in so many words.
- The lease form has a "Payment details" field for the method and details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Payment-method rules still apply.**
- The owner or agent must make a payment method with no extra cost available to you, other than your own bank or account fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- They must allow Centrepay and any prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- They must tell you about any costs of a payment method before you consent to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**4. You are entitled to receipts.**
- If you pay by transfer and ask for a receipt when you pay, you must get one within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The receipt must be signed. It must state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**5. Your bond.**
- The bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of the owner or agent receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The Regulations prescribe **electronic funds transfer** as a payment method that must be permitted. ## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**—the version in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you had **not entered into possession**, section 226 allowed you to terminate the tenancy by giving the landlord a **notice of termination** if the premises:

- were **not in good repair**;
- were **unfit for human habitation**;
- were unsafe;
- were not vacant;
- were not legally available as a residence; or
- were otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Damp, mould and rotting timber may support the “not in good repair” or “unfit for human habitation” grounds, but the documents do not say precisely when those conditions meet either test. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**; you were not required to enter premises that did not meet that requirement, and rent was not payable for the period before you actually entered into occupation if that requirement was not met. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had a continuing duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Terminate before moving in.**  
   Give the landlord a written notice of termination under **section 226**, stating that you have not entered into possession and relying on the premises being not in good repair and/or unfit for human habitation. Section 226 is the statutory route; the documents do not describe this as an automatic cancellation merely because you found defects. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs instead.**  
   Notify the landlord in writing, describe and photograph the damp, mould and rotting timber, and ask for the repairs. For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not repair within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; after receiving the Director’s report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

   If the rotting timber or other defect makes the premises **unsafe**, it may fall within “urgent repairs”, because urgent repairs included work needed to remedy a fault or damage making rented premises unsafe or insecure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for lower rent.**  
   You can ask the landlord to agree to a lower rent while the defects remain. The Act also allowed an application about **excessive rent**: the Tribunal could consider the premises’ state of repair and general condition when deciding what rent should reasonably be paid, and could order a refund of the difference from the date of your application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not state that rent was automatically reduced merely because defects were discovered before occupation.

Keep the notice, inspection records, photographs, condition report and all communications. Do not simply stop paying or treat the lease as ended without giving the statutory notice or obtaining the landlord’s agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Victoria), **Authorised Version No. 088**, which was in force on 15 October 2019, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about the situation
* **Landlord's Repair Duty:** The Act places a strict duty on landlords to ensure that rented premises are maintained in good repair . Furthermore, the presence of damp or mould caused by or related to the building structure is explicitly classified as an **"urgent repair"** under the legislation .
* **Condition on Move-in Day:** On the agreed day you are supposed to enter occupation, the landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition . If the premises do not meet this standard, you are legally not required to pay rent for the period between that agreed date and the day you actually move in .
* **Termination Before Possession:** The law allows a tenancy agreement to terminate if a tenant has not yet entered into possession and gives notice on the grounds that the premises are "not in good repair," "unfit for human habitation," or "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Cancel the lease:** Yes. You can give a formal notice of termination to your landlord before moving in, citing that the property is not in good repair or unfit for habitation due to the damp, mould, and rotting timber [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
* **Ask for repairs:** Yes. You can formally request that the landlord carry out the necessary work immediately. Because they are legally obligated to maintain the property in good repair, and because building-related damp/mould counts as an "urgent repair," you have strong grounds to demand immediate remediation , .
* **Lower rent:** The provided documents do not explicitly outline a process to request a lower rent before you have taken possession. ### 1. Written Notice of the Management Change
The owner must provide you with written notice of any change in management or contact details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). You should ensure this formal notification has been provided to you before making further payments.

### 2. Owner's Full Name and Address for Service
Because the agent is no longer managing the property, the owner (now acting as the residential rental provider) is legally required to give you their **full name and address for the service of documents** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

### 3. Emergency Contact Details
The owner must also provide you with an **emergency telephone number** to be used in case of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### 4. Payment Method Rights
Before paying, verify that the new payment arrangement complies with your statutory rights:
*   The owner must ensure at least one fee-free payment method (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
*   They must permit you to pay via **Centrepay** or another prescribed electronic funds transfer method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   You are entitled to receive a written receipt for your rent payment, which they must provide immediately if paid in person, or within 5 business days if requested at the time of payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### Summary of Action
Do not pay into the new account until you have received:
1. Written confirmation that the agent's role has ended and the owner is now managing it.
2. The owner's full name and address for service of documents.
3. An emergency contact number for urgent repairs.
4. Confirmation that a fee-free payment option (like Centrepay or direct bank transfer) remains available to you.

This ensures your tenancy rights are properly protected during the transition from agency management to private landlord management.

**Short answer:** Based on the Act as in force on 15 January 2026, the card fee is likely unlawful if it is charged for paying rent. The renter can insist on a fee-free method. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent matters in part, but the main prohibition applies to any person.

**What the law says**

- **Charges for electronic payment facilities are prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge in relation to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units. This is s 51(3)(b) in the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The text does not carve out agents or third parties, so it applies to the app company whichever party receives the fee. The documents don't define "electronic payment facility," so whether a card payment falls within it is a reading I'm inferring, not something the documents state.
- **Agents must offer a fee-free method.** A provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Bank transfer appears to be this kind of method, since the regulations prescribe electronic funds transfer as a payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how fast a method must be to count as "reasonably available," so the slower speed of bank transfer is not addressed.
- **Costs must be disclosed before consent.** The provider or agent must tell the renter about costs, "including third party transaction fees," that the renter may incur by using a particular payment method, before the renter consents to that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent-payment fees (not yet in force).** Section 51A bars non-exempt businesses from charging fees for prescribed matters, including "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)." Agents are exempt from s 51A, but the payments company is not listed as exempt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the list of prescribed matters in Regulation 21C only takes effect on 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So as of 15 January 2026, the documents do not show a prescribed rent-payment fee ban in force. The documents also don't identify any "other Act" that permits payment surcharges.

**What the renter can do or ask**

1. **Ask the agent for the cost details** of card payment, including any third-party transaction fee, before agreeing to pay by card [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

4. **Ask for a receipt.** If you request one at the time of payment, a written receipt must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Raise the card fee directly.** You can tell the agent that you are not willing to pay the app's card fee, given the s 51(3)(b) prohibition.

The excerpts don't show a separate "Authorised Version number" label, so "111" is the version number in the metadata.

## What the law says

- **A fee-free method must be reasonably available.** Under s 42(4), the provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own bank account don't count as additional costs. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your free bank transfer probably meets that test.** The Act doesn't say whether a slower free method is still "reasonably available", so the documents don't settle that point [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **You must be told about costs first.** Under s 42(7), the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a payment method before you consent to it. The Act lists "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" as examples [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **So on the text I retrieved, a card fee isn't banned outright.** It must be disclosed in advance, and the free option must stay reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **In s 42, no.** The excerpt doesn't distinguish between a fee kept by the agent and one kept by a third-party payments company. It expressly mentions third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Another section may matter more.** A later version, *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (in force from 13 Oct 2026, after your date), has these provisions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - **s 51(3)** says a person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent".
  - **s 51A** says a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent. The amendment notes show it was substituted by No. 46/2025.
- **I can't confirm those apply on 15 January 2026.** The v111 excerpts I retrieved don't include ss 51 or 51A, so I can't say what they provided in January 2026. I also don't have the Regulations in force on that date, so I can't say what is "prescribed" for s 51A. Attributing them to v111 would be a guess.
- **Why this matters.** s 51(3) is worded as "a person" and mentions electronic payment facilities. If it applied in January 2026, it could cover a card fee whoever receives it, which may make the app's fee unlawful.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for written disclosure.** Ask the agent to confirm in writing the card fee and who receives it. You're entitled to this before you consent (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use the free bank transfer.** The Act requires a no-extra-cost method to be reasonably available to you (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Say so if the free option isn't practical.** If the transfer is too slow or impractical for you, tell the agent. Whether that breaches s 42(4) isn't answered in these documents.
4. **Check ss 51(3) and 51A in the version in force in January 2026.** The documents I retrieved don't let me say whether they prohibit the card fee. This is the key open question.

The documents don't cover complaint or enforcement pathways, so I can't advise on those.

answer:
**Document applied:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I have not used the later versions (v089 onwards). The v088 file also contains amending text from a later Act, but I relied only on the operative text, which still uses "landlord" and "tenant" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Condition on the move-in day.** On the agreed day you were to enter occupation, the landlord must ensure the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition" (s 65(1)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **You can decline to move in.** A tenant is not required to enter into occupation of premises that don't meet s 65(1) (s 65(2)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No rent until you move in.** If the premises don't comply, you don't have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually enter occupation (s 65(3)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs.** The landlord must ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair (s 68(1)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Limit of s 65.** Section 65 speaks only of "vacant" and "reasonably clean". The retrieved text does not say whether damp, mould or rotting timber counts as not "reasonably clean". The rent and occupation protection in s 65 may therefore not clearly cover your problem. Section 68 (good repair) fits rotting timber better.

## What you can do

**1. Repairs**
- Give the landlord or agent written notice that repairs are needed. A tenant must also notify the landlord as soon as practicable of damage they become aware of (s 62) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord hasn't done the non-urgent repairs within 14 days, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. This must be within 60 days of receiving the Director's report (s 75(2)). If the Director hasn't reported within 90 days of your application, you can apply without the report (s 75(5)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the Tribunal finds the landlord in breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs, with a deadline (s 76) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For **urgent** repairs, you can arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to act immediately and couldn't. Give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost (s 72(2)(a)). The landlord is liable for the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72(2)(b)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the limit, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal, which must hear it within 2 business days (s 73) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- After giving repair notice, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord fails to carry out the repairs (s 77) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Lower rent**
- Section 65(3) relieves you of rent until you enter occupation, but only if the premises fail s 65(1) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Apart from that, the v088 text I retrieved has no general right to a rent reduction for defects. The nearest provisions are excessive-rent complaints to the Director, which apply where services or facilities were reduced or withdrawn, or where you've received a rent-increase notice (s 45) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a Tribunal excessive-rent order, "the state of repair and general condition" is one factor (s 47(3)(b)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That path depends on a Director's report (s 46) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and it doesn't clearly fit your situation.

**3. Cancelling**
- The retrieved v088 text has no provision on ending a lease before you take possession. Section 65(2) lets you refuse to enter occupation, but the text I found doesn't say it lets you end the agreement or get out of your obligations.
- I also did not find the Tribunal's compensation power (s 212) in the v088 text, so I can't say whether you can claim compensation.

**Next step:** on cancelling and compensation, the documents don't answer. Put your complaint in writing to the landlord or agent now, and get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before deciding whether to walk away.

**Short answer:** The documents don't say a renter must be home to let the inspector in. They also don't authorise, or prohibit, a $90 rebooking fee. They do cover the notice and entry rules.

**Documents used (law in force on 3 December 2025)**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf", version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The search also returned later versions (RTA v115 of 13 Oct 2026 and Regulations v009 of 30 Jun 2026). They post-date today, so I haven't relied on them.

## What the law says

- **Smoke alarms:** The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms are working, have batteries and are tested at least once every 12 months. Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Right of entry:** The provider or agent may enter, with the people needed for the purpose, between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, after notice under section 88 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice period:** Entry to carry out a duty under the Act (s 86(1)(c)) needs at least 24 hours' notice. A smoke alarm check most plausibly falls here, because it is a provider duty. Seven days' notice applies to valuation and routine inspections (s 86(1)(d) and (f)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your seven days' notice would satisfy either.
- **Notice contents:** The notice must be in writing and say why they want to enter. It must be sent by post or handed to you personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty:** You must "permit" entry that is made in accordance with this Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary says the same: you must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** Entry must be reasonable. They must not stay longer than needed without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to be there?

- The Act gives a right to *enter* within the notified window and a duty on you to *permit* it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say you must be present, and it doesn't say you can insist on being present. Nothing in it addresses an agent using their own key. So I can't say from these documents that your absence is a breach.

## Can they charge $90?

- Nothing in the retrieved provisions allows a fee for missing or rebooking an entry appointment.
- Nothing in them expressly prohibits one either. The only fee prohibition I found concerns fees for consenting to assignment or sub-letting, which doesn't apply here [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- So the documents don't answer this part. Check your rental agreement and the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance.

## What you can do

- **Check the notice:** It should be in writing, state the purpose, and be posted or personally delivered between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Agree another time:** The agent can enter at any time you agree to, if you consent within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the Tribunal:** You can apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting the days and times of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If they breach the entry rules:** You can apply to the Tribunal to restrain entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering without reasonable excuse outside the Division is an offence carrying 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

If the bond hasn't been lodged, the agent may need to hand over the bond or the lodgment before the changeover. ## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 111**, dated **25 November 2025**, in force on 15 January 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 005**, dated **25 November 2025**, also in force on that date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account—is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A bank-transfer option with no fee appears to satisfy that requirement, even if it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act also says that **“a person” must not demand or receive a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to the establishment or use of direct-debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) A card-payment fee charged by the app company may fall within that prohibition, but the retrieved documents do not expressly decide whether a particular card surcharge is such a prohibited charge. ## What the law said on 15 October 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. It was in force on 15 October 2019. The landlord had to provide premises that were **vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day**. You were **not required to enter into occupation** if they did not meet that requirement. If they did not, you were **not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually entered into occupation**. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had to maintain the premises in **good repair**. This duty applied even if you knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation, and regardless of the rent, age or character of the premises. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure was listed as an **urgent repair** where it made the premises unsafe or insecure. [[15]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not specifically classify rotting timber as an urgent repair, although it may support an argument that the premises are not in good repair or are unsafe. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to cancel the agreement by mutual agreement.** The documents do not give you an automatic right to cancel merely because you discovered damp, mould and rotting timber before moving in. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Give written notice requiring repairs.** For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not repair them within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director to investigate and then potentially to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the mould or damp is an urgent repair, you can require immediate action; if the landlord does not act, the Act allowed you to arrange the urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them, subject to the statutory procedure. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not move in while the problem remains**, if the premises do not meet the statutory requirements. You are not required to enter into occupation, and you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation if the premises do not comply with section 65. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for a rent reduction**, but it would need to be agreed with the landlord; the documents do not provide a general right to impose a lower rent before moving in. If repairs are not done, you may instead apply to the Tribunal for permission to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account**. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **If the premises are unfit for human habitation**, you may give a notice of intention to vacate specifying termination on the day of the notice or a later date. Whether the conditions you describe meet that legal threshold is not determined by the documents. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)

Preserve photographs, inspection reports and written communications, and write to the landlord or agent immediately describing each defect and stating that you have not entered into occupation.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 111 (in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation on January 15, 2026:

### What the law says about card fees
Under Section 42(4) of the Act, your rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs** (other than standard bank or account fees on your own bank account) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Since you have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, this legal requirement appears to be satisfied.

Regarding the card surcharge itself, Section 42(7) of the Act explicitly acknowledges that renters may incur **"third party transaction fees"** when using certain payment methods [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The law requires your provider or agent to give you clear information about these costs *before* you consent to use that specific payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). As long as a fee-free alternative is reasonably available and you were properly informed of the third-party card fee beforehand, the payments company is legally permitted to charge it.

### Does it matter who receives the fee?
No, it does not matter whether the fee goes to the agent or the third-party app company. The legislation specifically uses the term "third party transaction fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), which means the law anticipates and permits fees charged by external payment processors (like your rent app) rather than just fees charged directly by the landlord or agent.

### What you can do or ask
* **Verify the fee-free option:** Confirm with your agent that the manual bank transfer is indeed a "reasonably available" fee-free method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

* **Use the free option:** If you wish to avoid the surcharge, you are entitled to use the fee-free bank transfer method without penalty or delay from your landlord.

### 🚪 Moving In & Paying Rent
The landlord must ensure that on the day you are agreed to enter occupation, the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The landlord has a legal duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because damp, mould, and rotting timber affect the structural condition of the property, you can formally request these repairs from the landlord. If the landlord fails to address them, you may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the specified repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs, you can also apply to the Tribunal if the cost exceeds $1000 or if you cannot afford it yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The provided documents do not contain a specific provision that allows you to unilaterally ask for or receive lower rent before moving in due to property defects. However, if you have given notice requiring repairs and the landlord fails to comply with their duty, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a Rent Special Account instead of directly to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 📄 Cancelling the Lease
The provided documents do not explicitly outline a process or right to "cancel" a lease solely due to damp, mould, or rotting timber before moving in. Your primary statutory options under these documents are to decline to move in until the condition improves and to apply to the Tribunal for repair orders [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

Cancelling is probably available, but the documents I retrieved don't confirm which version of the cancellation provision applies on 15 October 2019.

**What the law says**

- **Condition on the day you take occupation:** The landlord must ensure that on the agreed day you enter occupation, the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition. If they don't comply, you are "not required to enter into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No rent before you move in:** If the premises don't comply, you are not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed day until the day you actually enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repair duty:** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair." The 2018 amendment text in the same document says the landlord must provide and maintain premises "in good repair; and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," and that this applies "whether or not the renter was aware of any disrepair... before entering into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** The definition of "urgent repairs" includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may also fall under the "unsafe or insecure" limb, but the documents don't say so expressly.

**Your options**

1. **Cancel:**
   - The amendment text in the document says a renter who has not entered possession may terminate by giving notice on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair" or "unfit for human habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The same text allows a renter to give a notice of intention to vacate where premises are "unfit for human habitation," with a termination date that may be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - However, that text appears in the endnotes amendment section, and the consolidated provisions listed in the table of contents (for example, s 226, "Termination by tenant before possession") were not in the excerpts I retrieved. I can't confirm from these documents whether the new wording was in force on 15 October 2019. Check this before relying on it.

2. **Ask for repairs:**
   - Give the landlord **written notice** of the damage as soon as practicable. The Act requires this of a renter who becomes aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to carry them out immediately and you cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The reimbursement terms have changed between the old and amended text. The old text caps reimbursement at the lesser of the reasonable cost or $1000, while the amendment text requires reimbursement of the reasonable cost within 7 days of written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because you have not moved in, this route may be less practical, and I would not carry out work yourself without advice.
   - **Non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice, and if the landlord does not carry out the repairs within 14 days, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs and the time for them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

3. **Lower the rent:**
   - You may pay no rent for the period before you actually move in, as described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - The Tribunal can also assess whether rent is excessive. In doing so it considers "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).    - The excerpts I retrieved do not include the full procedure for complaining to the Director or applying to the Tribunal about excessive rent (sections 45 and 46), so I can't set out those steps from the documents.

**Not covered by the documents:** Your specific lease terms, your bond, whether any lease break fee applies, and what happens to any rent you have already paid. The documents also don't say how the Tribunal would treat your situation given that you have not yet moved in. Before acting, get tenancy advice and keep photos, written communications and a dated record of the defects.

**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, the owner can't change how you pay rent just by sending new bank details. The change needs your agreement, and you should check the points below before paying.

## What the law says

- **Changing the payment method needs agreement.** The renter and the rental provider "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [1, *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 101, in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023]. The agent can't make this change alone, and the agent is also a "residential rental provider" under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment must be fee-free and reasonably available.** The provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed before you consent.** The provider must tell you about "any costs (including third party transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees and any other electronic payment facility fees)" before you agree to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay and electronic funds transfer.** Providers must permit Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [2, *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024].
- **Receipts.** Rent payments must be receipted in writing. If you pay electronically, the receipt is due within 5 business days of payment, if you request one at the time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and state your name, the premises, the date, the period covered, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** The provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider holds the bond on trust for you until it is paid to the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Form 1 says that if you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Transfer of the landlord's rights.** If the provider assigns or transfers their rights and duties, the provider and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether moving from an agent to an owner-managed arrangement counts as a transfer.

## What to check before paying

1. **Get the change in writing and agreed.** Ask the owner to confirm the new account in writing and agree to it as a variation of your lease. The Act requires agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Confirm who the owner is.** The rental provider's name, address and contact details are required in the agreement. The provider must notify you within 7 days if the agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about fees.** Ask whether the new method has any costs. The owner must tell you about them before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). There must also be at least one fee-free method available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the bond.** Ask for the bond lodgment details and confirm the bond was lodged with the Authority and that you have its receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Your bond is held on trust for you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Make sure you get receipts.** Confirm the owner will issue signed rent receipts for payments into the new account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check it's a valid transfer.** Ask whether the owner is taking over the rental provider's rights. If so, ask for the s 424 notice to the Authority and a copy for you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## Limits of the documents

The documents I retrieved don't cover how to verify bank account details or protect against payment redirect fraud. They also don't say whether an agent can stop managing a property, or what happens to the agency arrangement. For those points, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.
