## Short answer

On 15 January 2026, the documents I retrieved do not say outright that a card fee on a rent app is banned or allowed. The rules point in different directions on this. The fee-free bank transfer matters, and so does who receives the fee, but not in a simple way.

**Documents relied on:**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf". The metadata labels it version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf". The metadata labels it version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

I found no separate "Authorised Version" number in the text. The version numbers above come from the metadata. Both documents were in force on 15 January 2026.

## What the law says

- **A free payment method must be reasonably available.** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own account don't count as additional costs (s 42(4)). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Fees must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a particular payment method before you consent to it. This expressly includes third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees (s 42(7)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Electronic fund transfers must be permitted.** Under s 42(5), the agent must permit prescribed payment methods, and the regulations prescribe electronic funds transfer (reg 19). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The standard rental agreement form also notes that a fee-free method must be permitted. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- **Some charges are banned outright.** Under s 51(3)(b), "a person" must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The Act doesn't say whether a card-payment surcharge counts as a charge for using an "electronic payment facility". That is the main uncertainty. Section 42(7) also treats "third party transaction fees" as something a renter may incur, which suggests some fees may be allowed if disclosed. The documents don't reconcile the two provisions.
- **Slowness is not addressed.** The documents don't say whether a free method that is slower is still "reasonably available". I can't say that a slow free option does or doesn't satisfy s 42(4).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Section 42 binds the agent.** It applies to the provider or their agent, so the agent must ensure a free option exists and must disclose fees, even if a payments company runs the app. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51(3) applies to "a person".** It doesn't distinguish between the agent and the app company. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51A targets third parties.** A business other than the provider, the provider's agent or a bank must not demand or receive a fee for a "prescribed matter" relating to payment of rent. That is aimed at a third-party company like your app provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51A is not yet operative on your date.** The prescribed matters are in regulation 21C, which includes "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". Reg 21C only has effect on and after 31 March 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) So the documents don't show this prohibition applying on 15 January 2026. After that date it would matter whether the fee goes to the third-party company. The documents don't say which "other Act" permits surcharges.

## What you can do

1. **Use the bank transfer.** It has no fee, and EFT is a method the agent must permit. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm the card fee and who receives it. They must tell you about these costs before you consent to the method (s 42(7)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. **Ask the agent to confirm a fee-free method is reasonably available** under s 42(4). Say if the slower transfer causes you real problems, such as late-rent risk. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. **Query the fee under s 51(3)(b).** Ask the agent why a charge for using an electronic payment facility is permitted. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
5. **Check the rules again after 31 March 2026.** The regulations on third-party rent payment fees start then. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Note too that the regulations version I found was in force only until 9 February 2026.

The documents don't cover complaint routes or whether this particular fee is lawful, so you may want to check with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

It incorporates amendments as at 2 July 2019 and was in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), so it covers 15 October 2019.

## What the law says

- **Before possession:** A tenancy agreement terminates if the tenant has not entered into possession and gives the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair", "unfit for human habitation" or "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's repair duty:** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition on the move-in day:** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day. A tenant need not enter if they aren't, and owes no rent from the agreed day until actually entering (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That section covers vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text doesn't say it extends to damp, mould or rot.

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease**
- Section 226 fits your facts if you give written notice to the landlord. Its grounds are that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The notice must be given before you enter into possession.
- The documents don't define "entered into possession", so I can't say whether collecting the keys counts. Don't move in or stay there, and keep evidence such as photos and dates.
- If you had already moved in, s 238 would let you give notice of intention to vacate where the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date can be the day you give notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Outside s 226 and s 238, a general notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days (s 235). For a fixed-term lease it has no effect if it names a date before the end of the term (s 236) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can also end the lease by agreement with the landlord (s 217) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs:** These include a serious roof leak and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure. The listed items in this version don't expressly include mould, damp or rotting timber [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs you can arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act and can't. You must give 14 days' written notice of the work and its cost. The landlord must reimburse the lesser of the reasonable cost or $1,000 (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for an order, which must be heard within 2 business days, if you can't meet the cost, it exceeds $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice. If the landlord hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report, or earlier if no report arrives within 90 days of your request (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs within a set time (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** After giving notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into this account while the landlord fails to repair (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** If you paid a bond, the landlord must give you two copies of a signed condition report before you move in. Within 3 business days of entering you must return one copy, signed or endorsed to show any disagreement (s 35) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition, except for matters you disagree with or defects not reasonably discoverable on inspection (s 36) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents give no clear right to a rent reduction because of defects you found before moving in.
- You can complain to the Director that rent is excessive because the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or because you received a rent increase notice (s 45) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither fits your situation as described.
- If the Tribunal does consider whether rent is excessive, it can look at the state of repair and general condition of the premises (s 47(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A reduction would therefore have to be negotiated with the landlord, or a payment arrangement agreed.

The documents don't say which option is best for you. If the landlord disputes your notice, the Tribunal is the forum to resolve it. I'd get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before sending a termination notice.

# Smoke alarm check: entry notice and the $90 fee

**Documents used (in force on 3 December 2025):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", **Authorised Version No. 111**, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf". The retrieved text doesn't print an Authorised Version number, but its metadata lists version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**The notice looks valid.**
- A rental provider or their agent may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday. For a purpose under s 86(1)(c), they must give at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 86(1)(c) covers entry needed to carry out a duty under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider has a duty to ensure smoke alarms work, have batteries, and are tested at least every 12 months (s 68AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check therefore appears to fall under s 86(1)(c). That is my reading, because the Act doesn't say so in terms.
- Seven days' written notice exceeds the 24-hour minimum, and a weekday window of 10 am to 12:30 pm is within 8 am to 6 pm [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must be in writing, state why the agent wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. (s 88) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there?**
- The documents don't say a renter must be present. The right given is to "enter rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Your duty is to "permit" a person exercising a right of entry in accordance with the Division to enter (s 89(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard-form summary says you must allow entry where the rental provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say whether an agent may use their own key to enter while you are out. I can't confirm that from these documents.
- Entry must be in a reasonable manner, and the person must not stay longer than necessary without your consent (s 87) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?**
- Nothing in the retrieved Act or Regulations authorises a "rebooking fee" for a missed entry appointment.
- The charges the Act does address include key money and similar charges (s 51) and certain application and rent payment fees (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). None of these mentions a rebooking fee, so the documents neither allow nor expressly prohibit it.
- The smoke alarm testing duty sits with the rental provider, not the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** which provision lets them charge $90. The retrieved documents don't show one.
- **Ask whether presence is required.** If not, you can let entry happen without you. You can also agree a different time. Entry is allowed "at any time agreed with the renter" if you consent within 7 days before the entry (s 85(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal for an order limiting entry times.** You can do this under s 89(2)–(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If the agent enters without following the Division,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a specified period (s 91) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering otherwise than in accordance with the Division, without reasonable excuse, is an offence (s 91A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of this answer:** I found nothing in the retrieved documents on whether the fee is lawful in itself, or on whether your lease has an additional term about it. Check your own agreement. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' advice service can confirm the fee point.

**Documents used (both in force on 8 November 2022):**
- *rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 7 September 2022 and listed as version 101. It was in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Notice of the change.** If an agent acts for the owner, the owner must give you the agent's details in writing. If there is no agent, the owner must give you their full name, an address for service of documents and an emergency phone number. The owner must give you written notice of any change in that information before the end of 7 days after the change (s 66(2)–(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard lease form carries the same note: the provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the agent or provider details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing how rent is paid.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in your agreement (s 42(2)). The provider and renter "by agreement" may change that manner (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard form has a "Payment details" section in the agreement itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not say the owner or agent can change the account by notice alone.
- **Cost-free payment.** The owner or agent must make a payment method with no extra costs reasonably available, other than your own bank fees, and must permit electronic funds transfer (s 42(4)–(5); Regulation 19) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They must also tell you about any costs of a payment method before you agree to it (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** Whoever receives your rent must give a written receipt immediately if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of receiving the payment, if you ask for it when you pay. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is rent (s 43) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Records.** If no receipt is required, the receiver must keep a record for 12 months. They must give you a copy within 5 business days of your request (s 43(2)–(2A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025** (“the Act”), in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, dated 25 November 2025** (“the Regulations”), in force on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A fee-free manual bank transfer appears capable of satisfying that requirement, although the documents do not define precisely what “reasonably available” means. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also tell the renter about costs, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees, **before** the renter agrees to use that payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The Act prohibits a person from demanding or receiving a charge for the **establishment or use of a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not state whether a card transaction surcharge of the kind described is legally treated as a charge for the “establishment or use” of the facility, rather than a payment surcharge.

The newer provision that would prescribe **“rent payment”** as a prohibited fee expressly excludes “payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act”, but that regulation only takes effect on **31 March 2026**, not on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The documents therefore do not establish a separate, definitive ban on this card surcharge as at 15 January 2026.

### Does it matter who receives the fee?

The documents do **not** say that the result changes merely because the fee is paid to the payments company rather than the agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The obligation to provide a fee-free method and disclose third-party transaction fees is imposed on the residential rental provider or the provider’s agent, while the prohibition in section 51(3) applies to **“a person”**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) On the retrieved material, the payments company’s involvement does not by itself avoid those requirements, but the documents do not decide whether the particular company’s card fee is prohibited.

## What the renter can do or ask

You can ask the agent to confirm:

1. that the manual bank-transfer option is available as a genuinely fee-free rent-payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. the amount and nature of the card fee, including whether it is a third-party transaction fee; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. when and how that fee was disclosed to you before you agreed to use the app; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. whether the fee is for establishing or using the electronic payment facility, which section 51(3) prohibits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the fee-free transfer is not reasonably available, or the fee was not disclosed before you consented to the app, you can raise that with the agent and ask for the card fee to be removed or refunded. The retrieved documents do not specify a further complaint procedure or determine whether a refund must be made.

## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you have **not entered into possession**, section 226 allows the tenancy agreement to terminate if you give the landlord a **notice of termination** stating that the premises:

- are **not in good repair**;
- are **unfit for human habitation**;
- do not meet rental minimum standards; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord must ensure that the premises are maintained in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) On the agreed occupation day, the premises must also be vacant and reasonably clean; you are not required to enter premises that do not meet that requirement, and you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do not specifically say whether particular damp, mould or rotting timber automatically makes premises “unfit for human habitation” or “not in good repair”; that would depend on the condition and seriousness of the defects. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to terminate/cancel the agreement.**  
   You can give a written notice of termination under section 226, relying on the premises being not in good repair, unfit for habitation, below minimum standards, or otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) This is a statutory termination notice, rather than simply treating the lease as cancelled without notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask the landlord to repair the defects.**  
   Give written notice describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. The landlord has a duty to maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not repair within **14 days** after receiving written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; after the Director’s report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not move in or pay rent while the premises do not comply.**  
   You are not required to enter into occupation of premises that are not vacant and reasonably clean, and rent is not payable for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually enter into occupation if section 65 applies. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The document does not expressly state whether every damp, mould or timber-rot problem engages section 65, so that point cannot be decided from the documents alone. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for lower rent.**  
   The Act does not provide an automatic rent reduction merely because defects are discovered before moving in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You may negotiate a lower rent with the landlord, but the statutory “excessive rent” process requires an application to the Director and then, if appropriate, an application to the Tribunal; the Tribunal considers matters including the premises’ state of repair and general condition. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not state that this process automatically suspends or reduces rent before an order is made. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Keep photographs, videos, inspection reports and all written communications. The retrieved provisions do not specify a required evidence format, but they do require written notices for the relevant repair process. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101, in force from 7 September 2022** (“rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The rent must be paid at the place and in the manner specified in the residential rental agreement. The rental provider and renter may change the manner of payment **by agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) Therefore, a new bank account is not automatically binding merely because the agent emailed new details; the documents do not state a special procedure for changing bank-account details. The agreement must identify the rental provider and, if applicable, the agent. The rental provider must notify the renter within **7 days** if any of those details change. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also:

- make a **fee-free payment method** reasonably available, apart from fees charged by your own bank; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- permit payment by **Centrepay** and any prescribed payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, dishonour fees or electronic-payment-facility fees, **before** you consent to that payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Your bond is separate from rent. The provider must lodge it with the RTBA within **10 business days** after receiving it. The RTBA should issue a receipt within **7 days** of receiving the bond; if you have not received a receipt within **15 business days** after paying it, you may contact the RTBA. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

1. **Who the current rental provider and managing agent are**, including the changed name, address, phone number and email address. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **That the owner has taken over management** and that the new account is the account to be used for rent under your agreement.
3. **The effective date** of the change and the rent period covered by your next payment.
4. **Any payment fees**, and confirmation that a fee-free method remains available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
5. A rent receipt after payment if you request one. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 111, which was in force on 15 January 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about card fees & third parties
The Act does not ban third-party payments companies from charging card fees. Instead, it regulates how providers and agents must handle payment options:
* **A free option must be available:** The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than standard bank/account fees) is "reasonably available" to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
* **Upfront disclosure is mandatory:** Before you consent to use a specific payment method, the provider or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur, which explicitly includes "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who receives the fee?
No, the legality of the fee does not depend on whether it goes to the agent or the payments app. The Act specifically anticipates third-party charges by requiring disclosure of "third party transaction fees" before you agree to use a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This confirms that separate payment processors can legally charge fees, provided your provider/agent has told you about them upfront and kept a free alternative reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Check for proper disclosure:** Ask your agent to confirm they provided clear information about the card fee *before* you agreed to use the app, as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If they did not, they have breached their disclosure obligations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Stick to the free method:** You are fully entitled to continue using the manual bank transfer option. The provider is legally required to keep a no-cost payment method reasonably available at all times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Raise a dispute if needed:** If your agent pressures you to use the card-only option or refuses to accept the free bank transfer, you can raise this with VCAT as it violates the requirement to provide a reasonably available, cost-free payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088**, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔑 Cancelling the Lease
**Yes, you can cancel.** Because you have signed the lease but have not yet moved your belongings in or stayed there, you have legally "not entered into possession" of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

Under the Act, you can terminate the tenancy agreement by giving written notice to the landlord on the grounds that the premises:
* Are not in good repair; or
* Are unfit for human habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

Damp, mould, and rotting timber typically fall squarely under these grounds. Once you serve this notice, the tenancy agreement terminates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ Asking for Repairs
You can demand repairs before taking possession. The landlord has a strict duty to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, on your agreed move-in day, the landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

If the damp and rotting timber mean the premises do not meet these standards, you are legally entitled to refuse to take possession until the landlord fixes them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Asking for Lower Rent
**The Act does not allow you to ask for a rent reduction before you have taken possession.** However, you have strong financial protection: if the premises do not comply with the required condition on your agreed move-in day, **you are not required to pay any rent** from that agreed date until the actual day you enter and occupy the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

### 📝 Recommended Next Steps
1. **Document everything:** Take clear photos/videos of the damp, mould, and rotting timber.
2. **Give written notice:** Send a formal letter or email to your landlord/agent stating that you are terminating the tenancy under Section 226 because the premises are not in good repair/unfit for habitation, OR state that you will not take possession until the issues are rectified under Section 65.
3. **Keep proof:** Save a copy of your notice and any responses from the landlord.

*Note: This advice is based strictly on the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, as it stood on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you need to escalate this dispute, you may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders.*

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 002)**, which were in force on 8 November 2022, here is what you need to know:

### What the law says about changing management & payment details
* **Changing how rent is paid requires mutual agreement:** The manner of rent payment is set out in your lease. You and the rental provider can only change this by agreeing to it together [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
* **Change of agent to owner-management triggers notice requirements:** If the agent stops managing the property and the owner takes over, the owner (the residential rental provider) must give you written notice of their full name and address for service of documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must also notify you in writing of any changes to the contact or management details previously provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
* **Transfer of rights requires RTBA notification:** If the rights and duties under your tenancy are transferred from the agent/owner to another party, the provider must notify the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 5 days and give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
* **Receipts are mandatory:** Anyone receiving your rent payments is legally required to provide you with a written receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What you should check before paying into the new account
1. **Written confirmation from the owner:** Do not pay based on an informal message. Ask for formal written notice from the property owner confirming they are now managing the tenancy, along with their official name, address for service of documents, and the new bank details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Agreement to the new payment method:** Confirm that you formally agree to change the payment method from what was originally in your lease. The law requires both parties to agree before the manner of rent payment can be changed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Copy of the RTBA transfer notice:** Request a copy of the notice the provider has submitted to the RTBA regarding the assignment or transfer of rights under your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Bond status & contact details:** Verify that your bond remains correctly lodged with the RTBA in your name. The change in who manages the property does not affect your bond, but you should ensure the RTBA still has your correct current address and phone number.
5. **Availability of a fee-free payment option:** Regardless of the new bank account provided, the owner must ensure at least one fee-free payment method (other than your own bank fees) remains available to you, and you retain the right to use Centrepay or electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

Once you have received written confirmation of the management change, agreed to the new payment details, and verified the RTBA notification, you can safely pay into the new account. Always request a receipt immediately upon making the payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The law in force on 15 January 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111, which applies from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 005, also applies on that date, until 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **No charge for electronic payment facilities.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge, or an indemnity for a charge, relating to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card payment is very likely an "electronic payment facility," so this is the most direct provision.
- **Fees for rent payment.** A business other than a rental provider, the provider's agent, or a deposit-taking institution must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The app company is not one of the excluded parties, so this rule may also apply to it.
- **Fee-free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs is reasonably available to the renter. The only costs allowed are bank or account fees on the renter's own bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Information before you choose.** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

Not much, based on these provisions:

- The "no charge for electronic payment facilities" rule applies to any "person," so it covers the app company even though it isn't the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The fee-free method rule and the cost-disclosure rule bind the provider and agent. If the agent takes the fee, or lets the app run the payment with a fee, the agent is responsible for making a fee-free method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The fee-prohibition rule for rent payments excludes providers and agents, so an agent receiving the fee is less clearly caught by that particular section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the electronic payment facility rule still applies to "a person," so it is not a clear way out for the agent.

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent** in writing whether the card fee is charged by the app or the payment company, and what it is. The agent must have told you about these costs before you chose the card method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Use the bank transfer** if it is a fee-free method. Note that the Act requires a fee-free method to be "reasonably available," not that it be instant, so slowness alone does not make it unreasonable. The documents don't say how slow is too slow [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the agreement.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement, and the Regulations' standard terms refer to the provider's "preferred methods of payment" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If the agreement names only card payment, ask the agent how to pay without the fee.
- **Keep records** of your payments and any fees charged. Receipts are required for rent payments, and you can request them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Gaps in the documents

- The Act refers to a "prescribed matter" for fees, and to "prescribed" payment methods, but the retrieved text does not list them. I can't confirm whether a card surcharge is a prescribed fee under the Regulations.
- The retrieved documents don't cover how or where to complain, or what remedies are available.

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't include the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* text in force on 8 November 2022, so I can't confirm the Act's rent-payment rules as they stood then. The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) does cover that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and the Act provisions I describe below come from later versions.

**What the law says**

- **Payment methods:** The standard rental agreement form says the rental provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** "The renter is entitled to receive a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing details:** The form says the rental provider "must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes," which covers agent details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It also says the parties "must immediately notify the other party in writing if their contact details change" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The rental provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days. If the renter has no receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, they may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing payment method (later Act):** The current Act (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) says rent is payable "in the manner (if any) specified in the agreement," and that the provider and renter "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version 110 (in force 6 August to 24 November 2025) has the same wording [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm this applied in 2022.
- **Costs and receipts (later Act):** The provider's agent must give the renter information about any costs, such as third-party transaction fees, that the renter may incur by using a payment method before the renter consents to it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A written receipt must be signed by the person receiving payment and must state the renter's name and the rented premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What to check or ask before paying the new account**

1. **Ask for written confirmation** that the owner is now managing the property and that the agent is no longer acting. Under the form, the change must be notified to you in writing within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the change is agreed.** Under the later Act, a change in payment method is by agreement [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Don't treat an agent's email alone as agreement to change your payment arrangement.
3. **Confirm the account is fee-free for you** (apart from your own bank fees), and ask whether any costs apply before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm the bond was lodged** with the RTBA and check whether you have a receipt. Because you paid a week ago, the 15-business-day window may not have passed yet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Get a receipt for each rent payment** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
6. **Verify the bank details independently.** The documents don't address how to verify a payee, so I can't advise on that from them. As a general precaution, confirm the new details through a contact you already have, not only the email that sent them.

**What the documents don't cover**

- The text of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force on 8 November 2022.
- Whether the owner must give notice or go through any process to take over management.
- Whether the bank-detail change needed your written consent under the 2022 law.

You may want to check the Act version that applied in November 2022 directly, or ask a tenancy advice service such as Consumer Affairs Victoria.

## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111 (file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", dated 25 November 2025). The metadata shows it was in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026, so it covers 15 January 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't applied version 115 (13 October 2026), because it post-dates your question [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**1. A free payment method must be reasonably available (s 42(4)).** The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A fee-free bank transfer is likely to meet this. The Act doesn't say whether "reasonably available" takes account of speed, so I can't say whether "slower" matters.

**2. Fee disclosure (s 42(7)).** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, expressly including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**3. Charges barred for electronic payment facilities (s 51(3)(b)).** Section 51(3)(b) applies to "a person". It says no one may demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card fee charged through a rent app could fall under this wording. The Act doesn't define "electronic payment facility" in the text I retrieved, so I can't confirm it does.

**4. Rent payment fees by businesses (s 51A).** A person carrying on a business must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* in relation to the payment of rent. The exceptions are the rental provider, the provider's agent, and authorised deposit-taking institutions (banks and similar) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who receives the fee?

Possibly, but the documents don't settle it.

- **Fee goes to the payments company.** The company is a business that isn't the provider, the agent or (presumably) a bank. So s 51A would apply to it, but only if the card fee is a "prescribed matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The prescribed matters are set by regulations, and the regulations I retrieved are not the version in force on 15 January 2026. I can't confirm whether card fees are listed.
- **Fee goes to the agent.** The agent is carved out of s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but s 51(3) still applies to "a person", and the agent's duties under s 42(4) and (7) still apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51(3)(b).** It doesn't distinguish by who receives the charge, so the destination of the fee doesn't change it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Answer:** the retrieved documents don't give a definite yes or no. Section 51(3)(b) could prohibit the card fee, and s 51A could prohibit it if the regulations prescribe it. The documents don't confirm either point.

## What you can do

- **Ask for the fee information in writing.** Ask the agent to set out all costs of each payment method, including the card fee, as s 42(7) requires before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Use the fee-free bank transfer** if you want to avoid the fee. The agent must keep a no-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent to confirm** whether the card fee is a charge for an "electronic payment facility" under s 51(3)(b), and whether it is a prescribed fee under s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Raise it if the free option isn't reasonably available.** If the bank transfer is impractical for you, you can put that to the agent under s 42(4) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I can't say from these documents where to take a complaint, or which regulations list the prescribed matters in force on 15 January 2026.

answer:
# Damp, mould and rotting timber before moving in (as at 15 October 2019)

I applied the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088** (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019. Authorised Version No. 089 only starts on 4 December 2019, so I haven't used it.

## What the law says

- **Before you move in (s 65).** The landlord must ensure that on the agreed move-in day the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **If they aren't.** You are not required to enter into occupation. You also don't have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually move in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Ongoing repairs (s 68).** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**Caveat:** s 65 is worded around "vacant" and "reasonably clean". It doesn't mention damp, mould or rotting timber. Whether mould counts as "not reasonably clean" isn't answered in the documents I found. The s 68 good-repair duty is the clearer fit for rotting timber and damp.

## Your options

**1. Not moving in yet.**
- If s 65 applies, you can decline to occupy. You owe no rent for the period before you actually move in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**2. Asking for repairs.**
- **Written notice.** Give the landlord written notice of the non-urgent repairs needed. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **After 14 days.** If the repairs aren't done within 14 days of the notice, you can apply in writing to the Director (Consumer Affairs) to investigate. The Director must investigate, may negotiate arrangements for repairs, and must give you a written report. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Tribunal.** If you have the Director's report and are still not satisfied, you can apply to the Tribunal. You must apply within 60 days of receiving the report. If you haven't received the report within 90 days of applying for it, you can apply without it. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Tribunal orders.** If the Tribunal finds the landlord is in breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs. The order must state the repairs and the time to carry them out. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Rent Special Account.** After you've given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Urgent repairs.** You can arrange these yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and couldn't. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. You can also apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The definition of "urgent repairs" (s 3) wasn't in the text I retrieved, so I can't say whether mould or rotting timber qualifies.

**3. Asking for lower rent.**
- **Rent for the delay.** If s 65 applies, no rent is payable until you actually enter into occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Excessive rent.** You can complain to the Director about excessive rent only where the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or after receiving a rent increase notice. The Tribunal can then declare rent excessive, taking into account "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Neither trigger obviously fits your situation, so a general rent reduction for poor condition is not clearly available on these documents.
- **Compensation.** The text I found for this version doesn't give a Tribunal power to order compensation for the repair breach. The compensation wording appears only as a later amendment in the endnotes. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**4. Cancelling the lease.**
- The sections of this version that I retrieved don't set out a tenant's right to cancel or end the agreement for this reason. They only say you needn't enter occupation under s 65 and needn't pay the pre-occupation rent. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- I can't say from these documents whether you can terminate. I'd suggest checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenant advocacy service before you act, as getting this wrong could expose you to liability.

## Practical steps
- Put the defects in writing to the landlord or agent and keep photos and dates.
- Say clearly that you haven't taken occupation because of them.
- Keep your written notice for the repair process above.

**Documents used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The excerpt I retrieved doesn't show the words "Authorised Version No." I'm taking "101" from the file name and metadata.
- **Regulations:** the file metadata gives version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 Nov 2024, so it also covers 8 Nov 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** rent is payable at the place in the agreement. If no place is specified, it is payable at the rented premises. It is paid in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing the payment method:** the rental provider and renter "by agreement" may change how rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). My reading is that new bank details change the agreed manner of payment, so you can ask for the change in writing before you agree. The documents don't say this in so many words.
- **No-extra-cost option:** the provider or their agent must make sure a payment method with no extra costs is reasonably available to you. Your own bank fees are the only cost allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cost information:** they must tell you about any costs of a payment method before you consent to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** whoever receives your rent must give you a written receipt if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of a request made when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and must state [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf):
  - your name and the premises;
  - the date of receipt;
  - the period paid for;
  - the amount;
  - that the payment is for rent.
- **Records:** if no receipt is required, the person must keep a record of the payment for up to 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must provide it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Change of details:** the prescribed Form 1 agreement says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider's or agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This applies if your agreement is on that form.

## What you can check or ask

1. **Look at your agreement.** Check the "Payment details" and preferred payment methods in the standard terms (clause 8 of Form 1) and the rental provider and agent details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Compare them with the new bank details.
2. **Ask for the change in writing.** Ask for written notice of the new management arrangement and the new account. The 7-day notice rule in Form 1 supports this [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm who the new payee is.** Confirm that the account name matches the owner named in your agreement. The documents don't explain how to verify an account or detect fraud. I can't say more on that from them.
4. **Ask about costs.** Ask whether the new method has any fees and whether a no-extra-cost option is available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Request a receipt.** Ask for a receipt for each payment. Make the request when you pay, so the 5-business-day deadline applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check your bond.** The bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of payment. The RTBA sends a receipt. If you have no receipt within 15 business days of paying, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A change in who manages the property is a good reason to check that this receipt arrived.

The retrieved documents don't say whether the agent can stop acting for the owner mid-tenancy, or what happens to your rent if you pay the old account. For those questions I'd need further sources.

## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111**, in force from 25 November 2025. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost**—apart from the renter’s own bank or account fees—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Before the renter consents to a payment method, the rental provider or agent must provide information about costs, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge connected with the **establishment or use of an electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, a card fee charged for paying rent through the app is not permissible merely because the fee is charged by the payments company rather than the agent. The prohibition applies to **“a person”**, and the Act does not make the result depend on who ultimately receives the fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly address a payments company’s contractual relationship with the agent, but they do not provide an exception for third-party app operators. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The existence of a free manual bank-transfer option may satisfy the fee-free-payment requirement **only if it is “reasonably available.”** The documents do not define that phrase or say whether being slower makes a method unreasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

The renter can ask the agent or rental provider:

1. **Why the card fee is being charged**, and whether it is a fee for using the electronic payment facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. **For written information about all fees** before consenting to use the app. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. To confirm that the **fee-free bank-transfer method** is reasonably available and remains available without penalty. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. Whether the card fee will be **removed or refunded**, although the retrieved documents do not state a specific refund procedure or remedy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The relevant supporting document is also the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005**, in force on that date; its prescribed rental-agreement form states that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method, other than the renter’s own bank fees. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had to provide the premises **vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day**. You were **not required to enter into occupation** if they did not comply. You were also **not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually entered into occupation**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a continuing duty to maintain the premises **in good repair**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure was expressly included in the Act’s definition of **urgent repairs**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move in until the condition is dealt with.** The Act says you do not have to enter into occupation if the premises do not meet the statutory requirement. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Give the landlord or agent written notice immediately.** Describe and photograph the damp, mould and rotting timber, and state that you require the premises to be made safe and repaired. The landlord’s duty is to maintain the premises in good repair. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for urgent repairs.** Structural damp or mould may fall within the urgent-repairs definition. If the landlord cannot be contacted or will not arrange the repairs immediately, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to contact them; the landlord’s reimbursement liability was limited to the reasonable cost or **$1,000, whichever was less**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
   If you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than **$1,000**, or the landlord refuses to pay, you could apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the urgent repairs. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **For non-urgent repairs**, you could give written notice and, if the landlord did not repair within **14 days**, apply to the Director for an investigation. After receiving the Director’s report, you could apply to the Tribunal for a repairs order; the application generally had to be made within **60 days** of receiving the report. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask to cancel the lease by agreement.** The retrieved provisions do **not** state that a renter has an automatic right to cancel solely because defects are discovered before moving in. They also do not provide a specific cancellation procedure on these facts. Therefore, obtain the landlord’s written agreement releasing you from the lease and confirming any refund of rent or bond.

6. **Ask for lower rent.** You can ask the landlord to agree to a rent reduction, but the retrieved provisions do **not** establish an automatic right to reduced rent merely because you have not yet moved in. They do establish that no rent is payable for the period beginning on the agreed occupation day and ending when you actually enter occupation if the premises fail the statutory condition. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Keep paying nothing that the Act says is not payable, but do not simply treat the lease as cancelled without written agreement or a Tribunal order. The documents do not contain enough information to say that handing over the keys, without moving in or staying there, by itself terminated the agreement.

The rental provider must ensure that the smoke alarm is correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries and tested at least once every 12 months. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)

You must permit a person exercising a valid right of entry to enter. The prescribed rental agreement identifies both the **rental provider** and, if applicable, the **rental provider’s agent**, including their names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses.
