The agreement must also state the available rent-payment methods and payment details. You are entitled to a receipt confirming rent paid, and the rental provider must allow at least one fee-free payment method, as well as Centrepay or another electronic-funds-transfer method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** specifically state the procedure for changing from an agency-managed tenancy to owner management, or for changing the bank account into which rent is paid. They therefore do not establish, by themselves, that the new bank details are genuine.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Written confirmation of the management change**, identifying the owner as the rental provider and confirming that the agency no longer receives rent.
2. **Updated rental-provider and agent details**, if the details in your signed agreement have changed; the change should be notified within 7 days. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **Written confirmation of the new rent-payment details**, including the account name, BSB, account number and the date from which they apply, and a receipt for your payment. 4. **Confirmation that your bond has been lodged with the RTBA.** The rental provider or agent must complete and give you a bond lodgment form when the bond is paid, lodge the bond with the RTBA within **10 business days**, and the RTBA must issue you a receipt. Based on the law in force on **15 January 2026**, your rights regarding payment fees are governed by:
* ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997***, Authorised Version No. 111 (in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
* ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, Authorised Version No. 005 (in force from 25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

### 1. Can the app charge you a card fee?
Yes, the third-party payments company can technically charge its own processing fee for card transactions. However, **your rental provider or agent cannot force you to use it**. 

Under Section 42(4) of the Act, your provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with **no additional costs** (other than your own bank's account fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard lease form also notes that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method (excluding your own bank fees) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

Because you already have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, your agent is meeting their legal obligation by offering that fee-free alternative. You are entitled to use it without penalty.

### 2. Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter who collects the fee.** The law focuses entirely on whether *you* (the renter) incur additional costs, not who receives them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Whether the card surcharge is kept by the payments company or passed on to the agent is irrelevant to your right to a fee-free payment method. 

Additionally, under Section 42(7), your provider or agent must give you information about any costs (including third-party transaction fees) before you consent to use that specific payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If they haven't clearly disclosed this fee upfront, they may be failing to meet their disclosure obligations.

**What you can do:**
* Continue using the manual bank transfer option; it is legally protected as a fee-free method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

You can raise this with them in writing, citing your right to a reasonably available fee-free payment method.

### 🔑 Can you cancel the lease?
The retrieved documents **do not explicitly state a right to unilaterally cancel or terminate** a tenancy agreement solely because of property condition before moving in. You would need to seek specific legal advice or apply to the Tribunal for termination on other grounds, but the provided text does not cover this option.

### 🏠 Can you refuse to move in & avoid paying rent?
Yes. Under the law, a landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a **reasonably clean condition** on the agreed occupation day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
* If the premises do not meet this standard, you are **not required to enter into occupation** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* You are also **not liable to pay rent** for the period between the agreed move-in date and the day you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🔧 Can you ask for repairs?
Yes. The landlord has a legal duty to ensure the rented premises are **maintained in good repair** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould, and rotting timber generally fall under this duty. However, these issues do not qualify as "urgent repairs" under the 2019 Act (which covers things like burst pipes, gas leaks, or serious storm damage). Therefore, you must follow the **non-urgent repair process**:
1. Give the landlord **written notice** advising that repairs are required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. If the landlord does not carry out the repairs within **14 days**, you can apply to the Director to investigate whether the landlord is in breach of their duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. After receiving the Director's report, if arrangements still haven't been made, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the specified repairs within a set timeframe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Can you ask for lower rent?
You cannot unilaterally reduce your rent yourself. However, if you have given notice requiring repairs and the landlord fails to comply with their duty, you can **apply to the Tribunal for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a Rent Special Account** instead of directly to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will specify how long this period lasts before the funds are released to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 📝 Summary of your immediate options:
1. **Do not move in** until the damp, mould, and rotting timber are resolved. You will not owe rent for the time you wait [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

3. If they ignore or delay the request past 14 days, **apply to the Director** for an investigation, then to the **Tribunal** for repair orders or a Rent Special Account order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Which versions apply today (9 November 2026):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version **115**, in force from 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Fees for paying rent are restricted.** Under s 51A of the Act, "a person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to an application to enter into a residential rental agreement or the payment of rent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regulation 21C, effective from 31 March 2026, lists "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So a card surcharge for rent is caught unless another Act permits a payment surcharge. The retrieved documents don't identify any such Act.
- **A no-cost option must be available.** Under s 42(4), the provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your bank transfer may meet this, but the documents don't define "reasonably available," so whether a slower method counts is not settled by the text.
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Under s 42(7), the provider or agent must tell you about costs, "including third party transaction fees," before you consent to a payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Separate charge rule.** Under s 51(3)(b), a person must not demand or receive a charge "in relation to the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This prohibition has no ADI exception.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Not on the wording of these provisions. Section 51A and s 51(3) apply to "a person," not only the agent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The one carve-out is that s 51A does not apply to an ADI (an authorised deposit-taking institution, such as a bank). The documents don't say whether your payments company is an ADI. Even if it were, s 51(3)(b) would still apply. The agent's duties under s 42(4) and s 42(7) also apply regardless of who collects the fee [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing what the card fee is, who receives it, and the legal basis for charging it, referring to s 42(7) and s 51A.
2. Ask for a fee-free method, such as bank transfer, to be confirmed as available under s 42(4). Note that the documents don't say what "reasonably available" means in practice.
3. Ask whether Centrepay is available. The provider or agent must permit Centrepay under s 42(5) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. If you pay, ask for a receipt. Under s 43(1), a receipt must be given immediately for in-person payments, or within 5 business days if requested for other payments [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether you can recover card fees you've already paid.
- How to enforce these rules or complain. The documents set penalties (for example, 80 penalty units for a natural person under s 51A and s 42(4), and 400 for a body corporate) but don't set out a complaint procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Because this is a legal question, consider checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before taking formal action.

## What the law says

- **Notice:** A renter must give the landlord written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter's duty:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, and fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Renters must also leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning limits:** A landlord cannot require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started, or professional cleaning is needed to restore them to their starting condition, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Options before the lease ends

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the landlord or agent in writing about the break-ins and the damage to plumbing and wiring [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Electronic notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** Your landlord must carry out urgent repairs once notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the landlord doesn't act, you may arrange repairs yourself only if you have "taken reasonable steps" to get the landlord to repair immediately and they are unable to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

3. **If you pay for repairs yourself:**
   - You must give the landlord **7 days written notice** of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within **7 days** after receiving written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations state that reimbursement is available for reasonable cost "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, if the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or if the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

5. **End the lease early (possible but conditional).** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or have been "destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe." The termination date can be the date of notice or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If this applies, the landlord cannot claim rent foregone under the standard terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Whether your premises meet this test is a factual question the documents don't resolve.

   Otherwise, for a fixed-term agreement, a notice that specifies a termination date earlier than the end of the term is of no effect, unless the agreement has a specific early-termination clause [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check your lease for that clause.

6. **Cleaning.** If you can't clean because of the damage, document the situation in writing and notify the landlord. The landlord cannot require professional cleaning unless one of the conditions above applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The bond can cover cleaning costs if premises weren't left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the lease [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

7. **Bond exposure.** A landlord can claim from the bond for repair costs from damage "caused by the renter or a renter's visitor" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A "visitor" is someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglars would not normally be there with permission, but the documents don't address this directly. Keep your records of the break-ins.

- Whether burglary damage counts as renter-caused damage for bond or compensation purposes.
- Whether your premises are "unfit for human habitation" or "unsafe" enough to support early termination.
- How the lease-break fee cap ("no more than one month's rent for each year left") applies when only about three weeks remain [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Sources
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"), **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version in the documents, so I treat it as the one in force today (9 November 2026).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number. Only the file metadata says version "009".

## What the law says

- **Condition on moving in.** The rental provider must make sure the premises comply with the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in (s 65A(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould, damp and structure.** The minimum standards say each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure (Sch 4, item 8). The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof (item 7) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to repair.** The provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The definition includes a failure to comply with the rental minimum standards. It also includes any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Cancel the lease before moving in (s 91L)**
- The agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination on one of these grounds. The ones relevant to you are that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or do not meet the rental minimum standards [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Caveat 1:** the retrieved text does not define "entered into possession". You have the keys but haven't moved in, so check how that applies to you.
- **Caveat 2:** the retrieved text does not set out the form of a s 91L notice or a notice period. Put it in writing and say which ground you rely on.
- **Alternative:** s 91ZD lets a renter give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date can be the date of the notice [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard-form agreement also says the provider can't claim lease-break compensation where this section is used (clause 16.3 of Form 2) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That clause appears in the more-than-5-years form, so check your own agreement.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs.** Mould or damp tied to the building structure is listed as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the premises don't meet the standards when you take occupation, you can issue an urgent repair request (s 65A(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If the provider won't act, you may arrange the repairs yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them. The provider must reimburse reasonable costs within 7 days of written notice, up to the prescribed amount [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard form states that amount as $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
  - You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear it within 2 business days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rotting timber.** It isn't named as urgent. It may fall under "unsafe or insecure" or the structural-soundness standard, depending on the facts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If it's non-urgent:
  - Give written notice. If the provider hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate (s 74) or to VCAT (s 75) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT must hear a non-urgent application within 7 days. It can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person and award compensation under s 212(2) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After you give notice and the provider fails to repair, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account for a set period (s 77) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- I found **no provision in these documents that lets you simply reduce the rent** for this problem.
- Rent only accrues day to day (s 39) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed entry day, you don't owe rent until you actually move in (s 65(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Mould is not expressly mentioned in that section, so it may not apply to your situation.
- Withholding rent into the Rent Special Account (above) and compensation under s 76(1)(c) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) are the closest remedies the documents give. The text of s 212, which governs compensation, was not in what I retrieved.

## Practical points
- Document everything with photos and written notices. A condition report you give the provider is treated as notice of the defects in it (s 36(1A)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must return it within 5 business days after entering occupation (s 35(2)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Under the Regulations, a provider must disclose a repair notice about structural mould or damp received in the last 3 years [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information from the documents, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre can confirm how s 91L applies once you have the keys.

## What the law says

I relied on two documents: the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026). Both are the latest versions I retrieved before today, 9 November 2026. The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so the version numbers come from the documents' metadata.

- **You don't have to wait indefinitely.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if (a) they have taken reasonable steps to arrange for the provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) they are unable to get the provider or agent to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A broken tap with the water off is likely to count as "urgent".** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply, and a water-using fitting or fixture malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't mention taps specifically, so how it applies to yours is a judgment call.
- **The owner's "own tradespeople only" position.** The documents say nothing about a provider being allowed to limit repairs to their own tradespeople. The legal test is whether the provider or agent actually gets the repair done immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether two calls today count as "reasonable steps" isn't defined in the documents.
- **Who can do the work.** The standard rental agreement form says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says a suitably qualified person includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). In practice, use a licensed plumber rather than fixing it yourself.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** The form says to notify the provider in writing of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act requires written notice as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Say that you've phoned twice, that the water is off to the whole house, and that you will arrange a plumber if the repair isn't done immediately. This also records your "reasonable steps".
2. **Arrange the repair** if they still don't act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Send a second written notice.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim the cost back.**
   - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice. The Act caps this at the reasonable cost or a higher prescribed amount if one applies, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The standard form states the figure as up to **$2,500** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **If they don't pay within 7 days**, you can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If you can't afford the repair, or it costs more than the prescribed amount, or they refuse to pay**, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the urgent repairs to be done. The Tribunal must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The Tribunal must also consider whether you gave the required written notice when it decides compensation claims [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Documents used**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- These are the latest versions I found. I did not retrieve the 2024 versions, so I haven't checked what they said when your lease started.

## What the law says

- **Professional cleaning terms are prohibited unless they are in the standard form.** A lease must not include a term requiring the premises to be professionally cleaned at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form (s 27B(1)(d)–(e)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable (s 26A(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your pet clause is probably void.** The standard form's pet clause only deals with consent to keep a pet. It says nothing about carpet cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A carpet-cleaning requirement in an added pet clause is an extra term, so it likely falls within the prohibition. This assumes the clause is an additional term and not part of the standard form text.
- **What the standard form allows.** The standard-form clause (clause 11 of Form 1) says the rental provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  1. The premises were professionally cleaned immediately before the tenancy started, **and** you were told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking fair wear and tear into account.
- **Your general duty.** You must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same standard appears in the regulation and the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Your two caveats

- If the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told, the agent can require professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Check your condition report and move-in paperwork.
- If the carpets are genuinely not back to their starting condition, professional cleaning may be required under the second exception [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What helps show the carpets' condition

The condition report is the key document. The form says it helps resolve disputes over cleaning and damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Start-of-tenancy report.** You should have filled in, signed and dated it within 5 business days of moving in. Your comments and photos on floor coverings are the baseline [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos.** The form says to take photos at the start and the end of the tenancy. They should be dated, labelled, show the location or room, and include close-up and distance shots [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **End-of-tenancy report.** The agent must complete the final inspection and condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a chance to attend, and they must allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). For each item, they must note whether it is clean, undamaged and working. If an item has changed, they are advised to comment and take pictures [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own cleaning evidence.** Your own dated photos and any record of the cleaning you did are useful. The documents don't say anything about receipts for self-cleaning.

## What you can ask the agent

- Ask them to point to the lease term that makes the pet clause enforceable. Say you understand that professional cleaning terms outside the standard form are prohibited (s 27B) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask them to show, from the condition report, either that the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy or that professional cleaning is needed to restore them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Ask to attend the final inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A renter can apply to the Tribunal to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable (s 28) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't cover how a bond or compensation dispute proceeds once the agent claims against you. I haven't covered that process here.

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Notify the provider in writing now.** Describe the break-ins and the plumbing and wiring damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep photos and any police report. The documents don't say anything about police reports or insurance.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - If the provider won't act immediately, you can arrange the repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations put the direct reimbursement limit at $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is above the prescribed amount ($2,500), or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show the equivalent term for shorter standard-form leases.
5. **Cleaning.** Because you can only clean "as far as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), tell the provider in writing that the damage prevents proper cleaning. Keep photos of the state you left it in.

## What the law says

The premises must meet rental minimum standards. They must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also ensure the premises comply with those standards and are maintained in good repair and fit for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Mould or damp related to the building structure is expressly included in the Act’s definition of **urgent repairs**; a failure to comply with rental minimum standards is also an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Rotting timber may indicate that the premises are not structurally sound, but the retrieved documents do not specifically address rotting timber.

The fact that you have collected the keys but have not moved in does not, by itself, appear in the retrieved documents as a right to cancel the signed agreement. The standard agreement says that if a renter ends the agreement early, the rental provider may seek compensation for actual rent lost, capped at **no more than one month’s rent for each year remaining**, and must take reasonable steps to re-let the premises or otherwise minimise the loss. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move your belongings in, and document everything.** Take dated photographs and videos of the mould, damp and timber, and keep all communications. The condition report is intended to record the premises’ state before occupation, and defects or outstanding repairs recorded in it count as notice to the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Write immediately to the rental provider or agent.** State that the premises do not appear to meet the structural-soundness, weatherproofing, mould-and-damp, and fit-for-occupation requirements; attach the evidence; and request that the agreement be ended by mutual written agreement, with any bond and rent paid returned. The retrieved documents do not state that the provider must agree to cancel on that basis.

3. **Ask for repairs.** You can require the provider to address the defects. For urgent repairs, you must first take reasonable steps to have the provider or agent arrange them immediately; if that fails, you may arrange the repairs, give **7 days’ written notice** of the work and cost, and seek reimbursement of the reasonable cost, subject to the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Regulations prescribe **$2,500** as the amount relevant to a renter’s application to the Tribunal for urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

4. **Apply for an order if repairs are not done.** For non-urgent repairs, give written notice; if the provider has not carried them out within **14 days**, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask for lower rent, but do not assume you are entitled to it automatically.** The retrieved documents do not provide a specific right to reduce the agreed rent merely because defects were discovered before moving in. You may negotiate a temporary or permanent rent reduction, or seek compensation, but any agreement should be in writing. The Act does provide for compensation where the provider is in breach and, in some repair situations, allows the Tribunal to authorise rent being paid into the **Rent Special Account** rather than directly to the provider; that is not the same as unilaterally paying less rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

6. **Do not simply stop paying or treat the lease as cancelled without advice.** If the provider will not agree to end the agreement, ending it yourself may expose you to a claim for rent actually lost, subject to the agreement’s limits and the provider’s duty to minimise the loss. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not contain a general pre-move-in cancellation right for this situation.

## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, current **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**, a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim must be made in an Authority-approved form. A renter’s signature is specifically required where the claim is a **joint claim** allocating part of the bond to the rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not say that a renter’s agreement to a proposed bond deduction, by itself, is the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice.

The Act allows a rental provider to seek compensation for loss or damage arising from a failure to comply with the rental agreement or the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the return of the full bond does **not, by itself, establish that no cleaning claim can ever be made**; the documents do not state that repayment of the bond bars a separate compensation claim. However, they also do not say that a later invoice is automatically payable merely because the renter previously agreed that an amount could be taken from the bond. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Any professional-cleaning requirement must also comply with the prescribed rules: professional cleaning may generally be required only where it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, taking account of the condition report and fair wear and tear, or where professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy and the renter was told about it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You do **not have to assume that the invoice is automatically enforceable**. Ask the agent to provide:

- the condition report and evidence that the premises were not left reasonably clean;
- the cleaning invoice, receipt or other evidence of the actual reasonable cost; and
- the legal or contractual basis on which they say your earlier agreement to a bond deduction also created a separate obligation to pay an invoice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can state that your agreement concerned a **possible deduction from the bond**, that no bond claim form was signed, and that the full bond was subsequently repaid. Whether your particular communication amounted to a separate binding agreement to pay remains a factual and contractual question that the retrieved documents do **not** answer.

If the agent insists on payment, you can dispute the invoice and ask the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal to determine whether compensation is payable and, if so, the reasonable amount. The Act permits the Tribunal to make a compensation order where a party failed to comply with the residential rental agreement or the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not provide a specific deadline for the agent’s separate cleaning invoice in these circumstances. Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (version 115, in force today) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about rent payment fees
Under section 42 of the Act, your rental provider or their agent has two main legal obligations regarding how you pay rent:

1. **A fee-free option must be available:** The law states that *"a residential rental provider or that person's agent must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **You must be informed of costs upfront:** The law requires that *"the residential rental provider or that person's agent must give the renter information about any costs (including third party transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees and any other electronic payment facility fees) that the renter may incur by using a particular payment method before the renter consents to use the payment method"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 1. Can the app charge you the card fee?
**Yes, but only if your fee-free bank transfer option remains available.** 
The law does not ban third-party transaction fees outright. However, because your agent is legally required to keep a no-cost payment method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), they cannot force you to use the card-paying app. As long as the manual bank transfer option remains open and accessible, the app's card fee is permissible.

### 2. Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter who receives the money.** 
The law focuses entirely on **the cost to you**, not who pockets the surcharge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the payments company keeps the card fee or passes it on to your agent is irrelevant under tenancy law. The only legal requirements are that a genuinely fee-free alternative exists for you and that you are transparently informed of any third-party transaction fees before you agree to use them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
* **Stick to the free method:** You are fully within your rights to continue using the manual bank transfer option. 
* **Ask for transparency:** If you ever choose to use the card app, ask your agent to confirm in writing that they will disclose any third-party transaction fees before you consent to the payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Report non-compliance:** If your agent removes the fee-free bank transfer option or pressures you into using a paid method, they are breaching section 42(4) of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can raise this with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today (9 November 2026), here is how your situation is addressed:

**Applicable Documents & Versions:**
*   *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version v115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version v009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔍 The Law on Property Condition
Under the current regulations, your landlord has strict legal obligations regarding the condition of the premises at the start of a tenancy:
*   **Rental Minimum Standards:** Every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure, and the premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber and structural mould/damp are direct breaches of these standards.
*   **Landlord's Duty:** The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards, remain vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and maintain the property in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 📋 Your Options

**1. Can you cancel the lease before moving in?**
The provided documents do not explicitly state a statutory right to unilaterally cancel a residential rental agreement *before* you have moved in due to disrepair. However, because the landlord is legally required to provide premises that are structurally sound and free from structural mould/damp at commencement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), you may be able to negotiate an early termination or seek remedies under general contract/consumer law (which the regulations acknowledge applies) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should formally notify the agent/landlord in writing of the defects immediately.

**2. Can you ask for repairs?**
Yes. Once the tenancy begins, damp and mould caused by the building structure are legally classified as **urgent repairs** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Urgent Repairs:** You must notify the landlord in writing. They are required to carry out these repairs immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they fail to do so after you have taken reasonable steps to contact them, you may arrange the repairs yourself and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs (up to $2,500) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), or apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to fix it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
*   **Non-Urgent Repairs:** For other structural issues (like rotting timber not deemed immediately urgent), you must give written notice. The landlord has 14 days to complete the repairs. If they do not, you can apply to the Director or VCAT for a compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Can you ask for lower rent?**
The provided documents do not allow you to unilaterally reduce your rent. However, if you have given written notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** while the repair dispute is being resolved [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Additionally, if VCAT finds the landlord breached their duty to maintain the premises in good repair, the Tribunal can order the landlord to pay you compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### ✅ Recommended Immediate Steps
1.  Take dated photos of the damp, mould, and rotting timber.
2.  Send a written notice (email or letter) to the agent/landlord immediately stating that the premises do not meet the rental minimum standards for structural soundness and are free from structural mould/damp [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3.  Clearly state whether you wish to negotiate an early termination of the lease before moving in, or if you intend to proceed with the tenancy and require urgent repairs under section 72 of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

You are permitted to attach these photos directly to your copy of the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v009)**, which are in force today, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔹 The Law on Bond Claims & Cleaning
Under Victorian law, a rental provider can only access money from a bond by lodging a formal claim with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) using an approved form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While a provider is entitled to claim the reasonable cost of cleaning if the premises were not left reasonably clean (accounting for fair wear and tear), this must be done through the official bond claim process while the money is still held by the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Once the RTBA has repaid your full bond to you, their statutory role in that tenancy ends. The law explicitly states that no further claims can be made against the Authority or the Residential Bonds Account once a bond has been paid out in good faith [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because you never signed a bond claim form and received your full refund, the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from the bond.

### 🔹 Is Agreeing to a Bond Deduction the Same as Agreeing to Pay an Invoice?
**No.** They are legally distinct mechanisms:
* **A bond deduction** is a specific statutory process for accessing funds already held by the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **An invoice** is a commercial request for payment outside of the bond scheme.

Agreeing to have money taken from your bond does not automatically mean you agreed to pay a separate invoice later. Unless your tenancy agreement or a separate written contract explicitly states that any cleaning costs will be invoiced separately if they are not covered by the bond, agreeing to a bond deduction does not create an obligation to pay a later invoice. 

Additionally, under the regulations, a provider can only require you to pay for professional cleaning if it was carried out at the start of your tenancy or is strictly necessary to restore the premises to their original condition (accounting for fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 🔹 What You Can Do
1. **Review your paperwork:** Check your original tenancy agreement and any written correspondence to see if you explicitly agreed to pay a separate invoice for cleaning costs. 
2. **Respond in writing:** If you did not agree to an invoice, reply to the agent stating that you only agreed to a bond deduction (which was never processed) and that you do not accept liability for a separate invoice.
3. **Check the condition report:** If the agent claims the cleaning was necessary, they must prove the premises were left unreasonably dirty compared to the initial condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
4. **Dispute if necessary:** If the agent continues to demand payment or threatens legal action, you can seek free advice from the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or a community legal centre regarding contract and tenancy law.

*Note: This information is based on the current statutory framework. It does not constitute formal legal advice.*

- **A free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Before the renter agrees to a payment method, the provider or agent must give information about any costs, including third-party transaction fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Ongoing repair duty.** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies whether or not you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Your situation matters here. The Act uses "entering into occupation," so whether you have already entered occupation (having keys alone may not be enough) is a question the documents do not answer. Get advice on that point.

- You are "not required to pay rent" for the period from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- The Regulations add that the provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

So the key question is whether professional cleaning is actually *required* to restore the carpets. If your own cleaning restored them to their starting condition, the documents suggest professional cleaning may not be required.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Check the condition report.** The renter must fill in their part within 5 business days after moving in, and the report "may help the renter verify the condition of the rented premises, if there is a later dispute about the renter's responsibility for damage or cleaning" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Gather photos.** The form advises taking photos "at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy," dated and labelled by location [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Photos are useful in a dispute about condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Check the end-of-tenancy inspection.** The provider must complete the final inspection and condition report "within 10 days after the end date of the agreement," give the renter an opportunity to attend if possible, and "allow for fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Dispute the requirement.** A renter can apply to VCAT for an order declaring a term invalid or varying it if it is "harsh or unconscionable" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Act also lets VCAT declare a term invalid where it is a prohibited term [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents do not cover**

- They do not say whether a renter must provide a receipt from a professional cleaner, or whether a self-cleaned carpet can be treated as meeting the clause.

**Short answer:** The current Act gives you a few routes. You should report the damage in writing now, ask the landlord to repair, and arrange urgent repairs yourself if they don't act. If the premises are unfit or unsafe, you may be able to end the tenancy on short notice. The general notice route won't help you break the lease early. The documents don't cover burglary-specific issues, insurance, or police reporting.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf), in force from 13 October 2026. It is the latest version in the retrieved set and has no end date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Duty to report:** You must give the landlord written notice as soon as practicable after you become aware of damage to the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72AA). The notice must state the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62).
- **Duty not to damage:** You and your visitors must not intentionally or negligently cause damage, but fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61). The documents don't say whether burglars count as "visitors" or how liability applies to a break-in. A repair notice can be issued where damage results from your failure to take care [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 78).
- **Condition at the end:** You must leave the premises, "as far as practicable," reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(2)). The documents don't say how this applies when damage prevents cleaning.
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to have the landlord do them immediately and they haven't. You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72). The Act caps reimbursement at the lesser of the reasonable cost or a prescribed amount. An expired regulations version stated $2,500 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so check the current figure. The documents don't include the s 3(1) definition of "urgent repairs," so I can't confirm that plumbing or wiring damage qualifies.
- **VCAT:** If you can't pay for urgent repairs, or the landlord refuses to reimburse you, you can apply to VCAT. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 73).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If the landlord doesn't act within 14 days of written notice, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (ss 75, 74).

### Ending the lease early

- **General notice:** A notice of intention to vacate must give at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91Z). With about three weeks left, that period would run past the end of the lease. A notice that sets a termination date earlier than the end of the fixed term has no effect in any other case [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZA(1)(b)).
- **Unfit or unsafe premises:** You may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed to an extent that makes them unsafe. The termination date can be the date the notice is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD). This is the most relevant route if the wiring is unsafe.
- **Lease-break fees:** The text I retrieved says no lease-break fee applies to terminations under s 91ZB or s 91ZC [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't say whether that applies under s 91ZD, so I can't confirm it.
- **Reduced notice (14 days):** The categories in s 91ZB don't include damage from a break-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do now

1. **Notify in writing today.** List each damaged item, when you found it, and what it is. Keep copies and photos.
2. **Get a professional assessment** of the plumbing and wiring. This supports both an urgent-repair request and any claim that the premises are unsafe.
3. **Ask the landlord in writing** to carry out urgent repairs, and give a reasonable deadline.
4. **If they don't act,** arrange urgent repairs yourself and send the 7-day written notice with the cost. An expired regulations version states that only a suitably qualified person may carry out repairs [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so use a licensed tradesperson.
5. **If the wiring or plumbing makes the home unsafe,** consider a s 91ZD notice of intention to vacate.
6. **Clean what you can** and keep records showing what you couldn't do because of the damage.
7. **If there's a dispute,** apply to VCAT for urgent repairs or reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover insurance claims, police reports, or how a burglary affects liability. **Version caveat:** I can't confirm which version is in force today, 9 November 2026. The newest Act version I retrieved is *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Version 111 (dated 25 November 2025), which shows an in-force period ending 29 June 2026 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Later versions are not in the documents. The rules below are the same in every version I retrieved, but check them against the current versions. For a lease that started in 2024, the Regulations then in force were Version 002 (dated 1 June 2022, in force to 30 November 2024), which has the same wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve an Act version dated for 2024.

## What the law says

- **Professional cleaning terms are generally prohibited.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **A prohibited term is void.** If an agreement contains a prohibited term, it is "void and unenforceable" [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form allows only a limited cleaning term.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
  1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and the renter was told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear".
- **The renter's duty is the same test.** The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if cleaning becomes required to restore them to their starting condition, again by reference to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets.** The standard-form pet clause only deals with seeking the rental provider's consent to keep a pet. It says nothing about carpet cleaning [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents contain no pet-specific or carpet-specific cleaning rule.

**Applied to you:** A pet clause that flatly requires professional carpet cleaning looks like an extra term of the kind s 27B(1)(d)–(e) prohibits, so it would be void [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Under the standard-form test, the agent can only insist on professional cleaning if the carpets actually need it to match their starting condition, or if they were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told. If the carpets are back to how they were, the documents give no basis for requiring a receipt.

## What you can do or ask

- **Rely on the condition report.** The law measures the carpets against the condition report [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The standard form says you must be given 2 copies (or one emailed copy) on or before the day you move in [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Compare the carpet entries in that report with their condition now.
- **Ask the agent which basis they rely on.** Ask whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before your tenancy and whether you were told, or whether they say the carpets need cleaning to match the condition report. The agent has to show one of these [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal if needed.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Evidence:** Apart from the condition report, the retrieved documents don't say what else counts as evidence of the carpets' condition, such as photos or cleaning records. I can't say more on that from these sources.

## What the law says

- **Unfit or unsafe premises:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe. The termination date can be the day you give the notice or any later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZD).
- **Ordinary notice doesn't help here:** A normal notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91Z). On a fixed term, it has no effect if it ends the agreement before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZA). With about three weeks left, that route adds nothing.
- **Landlord's duties:** The rental provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 26). The rental provider must also carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 30).
- **Your duties:** You must notify the rental provider in writing of damage to the premises, and keep the premises reasonably clean [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 25).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing now.** Describe the burglaries and the plumbing and wiring damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 25, 31).
2. **Request repairs.**
   - Urgent repairs: the rental provider must act once notified. If you've taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to do them immediately and they haven't, you may arrange them. You can be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500. You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the rental provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 30).
   - Non-urgent repairs: you can apply to VCAT if they aren't done within 14 days of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 31).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, so don't fix the plumbing or wiring yourselves [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 29).
3. **Consider ending the tenancy early under s 91ZD.** This is only available if the premises are truly unfit for habitation or unsafe, which depends on the facts. Damaged plumbing and wiring may support it, but the documents don't say whether this damage qualifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can name the same day or a later date. Keep photos and any tradesperson's report.
4. **Expect a possible notice from the other side.** The rental provider has the same ground and can also give notice to vacate for unfit or unsafe premises, effective the same day or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZL).
5. **Repeated break-ins and locks.** The rental provider must ensure the premises have window locks and deadlocks that meet the rental minimum standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (cl 28). - Whether the plumbing and wiring damage counts as an "urgent repair". The regulations point to the Act's definition in s 3(1), which isn't in the retrieved text [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- Any hardship application to VCAT. I only found s 91U in a 2019 version, not the current one, so I can't confirm it applies today.

The version in force today (9 November 2026) is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". ## What the Act says

- **Cleaning is a permitted bond claim, within limits.** A rental provider (which includes an agent) may claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter". That is judged against the condition of the premises at the start of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent must give you evidence first.** At least 3 days before a claim to take bond money is made, the provider or agent must give each renter bond claim evidence supporting the claim. That evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Undisputed claims are paid out.** The Authority repays the bond where the claim is joint, or where the provider claims repayment to the renter, or where nobody disputes the claim within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal applications about the bond have a deadline.** An application to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order must be made within 14 days after the agreement has terminated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to pay the invoice?** The documents I retrieved do not say. They cover claims against the bond. They don't say whether an agent can invoice a former renter separately after the full bond has been refunded. I can't answer that from them.

**Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?** The documents don't say either. The Act treats a deduction as a bond claim, made on an approved form with supporting evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Nothing in the retrieved text turns an informal agreement about a deduction into a separate debt. Nothing in it rules that out either.
