- **Ask the agent for the evidence.** Request the cleaning evidence and the condition reports. The 3-day evidence rule is written for bond claims [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The same test is a sensible benchmark for the invoice: was the place not left reasonably clean compared with how it started, and is the cost reasonable? The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also provide premises that meet the minimum standards, are reasonably clean, in good repair and fit for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Structural mould or damp is expressly an **urgent repair**, as is any fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure; the Act specifically includes mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

### 1. Cancel the agreement

Because you have not moved in or stayed there, you may be able to give a **written notice of termination before entering into possession**. Section 91L allows this where the premises:

- are not in good repair;
- are unfit for human habitation;
- do not meet a rental minimum standard; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Damp, mould and rotting timber may engage those grounds, but whether the condition is sufficiently serious—particularly whether the premises are “unfit for human habitation”—would depend on the evidence. The documents do not define that threshold. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed agreement says the rental provider cannot claim rent foregone for early termination where the renter terminates under section 91ZD because the premises are unfit for habitation or destroyed/unsafe. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) However, that clause refers to section 91ZD, while your situation before possession is addressed by section 91L; the documents do not expressly state whether the same protection applies to a section 91L termination. **Do not simply stop paying without giving a formal written notice or obtaining agreement.**

### 2. Ask for repairs

You can notify the rental provider or agent **in writing**, describing each defect and attaching dated photographs or reports. The provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

If the provider does not act, the documents say that a renter may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them immediately, and may seek reimbursement of reasonable costs up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do not explain whether arranging repairs yourself before entering possession would be appropriate, so do not authorise substantial structural work without written agreement or advice.

For non-urgent repairs, the provider must act within a reasonable time; a renter may apply to VCAT if repairs have not been completed within **14 days** after written notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Because structural mould/damp is expressly classified as urgent, the urgent-repair pathway is the more relevant one here. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### 3. Ask for lower rent

You may ask the rental provider to agree in writing to a lower rent while repairs are completed. The documents do not provide an automatic right to unilaterally reduce the rent simply because the premises are defective.

You may instead seek compensation for loss or damage caused by the provider’s failure to comply with the agreement or the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may order compensation, and that compensation may take the form of a **refund or reduction of rent**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

### Practical next step

Send a written notice immediately stating that you have not entered into possession, identifying the mould, damp and rotting timber, attaching evidence, and either:

1. **terminating under section 91L**, if you do not want the property; or  
2. requiring urgent repairs and asking for a written timetable and an agreed rent reduction while the premises are unavailable.

Do not sign a condition report describing the defects as acceptable, and do not move belongings in before deciding which option you will pursue.

Damage that makes rented premises **“unsafe or insecure”** is an urgent repair. The Act’s urgent-repair definition includes a dangerous electrical fault, failure of electricity or water, and any fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, and repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the premises are **unfit for human habitation**, or have been destroyed totally or enough to be unsafe, you may give the rental provider a written notice of intention to vacate. The termination date can be **the date the notice is given or a later date**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The notice must be in writing and signed. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

For the prescribed fixed-term agreement, the rental provider is not entitled to rent foregone when the agreement ends because the renter gives notice under section 91ZD on the basis that the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately notify the rental provider or agent in writing** of the burglary damage, especially the plumbing and wiring damage, and state that the premises may be unsafe or unfit for habitation. Renters must report damage and breakdowns as soon as practicable. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Request urgent repairs immediately.** If you have taken reasonable steps to arrange them but the rental provider or agent does not do them, you may arrange urgent repairs yourself. The rental provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving written notice of the repairs and their cost, subject to the prescribed limit. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not state the current prescribed dollar limit in the Act text, although the agreement form refers to reimbursement up to **$2,500**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. If you cannot pay, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the rental provider refuses to pay, **apply to VCAT for an urgent-repairs order**; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. If the premises are genuinely unfit or unsafe, **give a section 91ZD notice of intention to vacate** and specify an immediate termination date or a later date. On the documents available, this is the clearest way to end the fixed term without liability for rent foregone under the agreement form. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

5. Alternatively, you and the rental provider can agree in writing to end the fixed term early. The documents also allow either party to apply to VCAT to reduce or terminate a fixed-term agreement for **severe hardship**, but compensation may be ordered. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) You should therefore ask the rental provider in writing to confirm that cleaning affected by the unrepaired plumbing and wiring damage will not be treated as renter-caused damage, or seek a VCAT order if they refuse. **What the law says**
Under the Victorian residential tenancy laws currently in force today, the rules for professional cleaning are found in:
* **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v005) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
* **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version v115) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The standard form lease explicitly states that a rental provider cannot require you to arrange or pay for professional cleaning at the end of your tenancy unless it is actually *required* to restore the carpets to the condition they were in immediately before you moved in, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This statutory rule is supported by section 27C of the Act, which permits this term only if professional cleaning becomes necessary to achieve that restoration [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because your legal obligation is tied to the *result* (the condition of the carpets) rather than the *method* (who cleaned them), you do not have to pay for a professional cleaner or provide a receipt if your DIY cleaning successfully restored them to their original state.

**What the renter can do or ask**
1. **Reference the Condition Report:** The law requires the agent to give you two copies of the condition report on or before your move-in date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Use this document as your primary evidence to show that the carpets are back to their starting condition (minus fair wear and tear).
2. **Provide Photographic Evidence:** If you took photos when you moved in, share them alongside photos of the cleaned carpets to prove they match the original state.
3. **Communicate with the Agent:** Politely inform the agent that under clause 12 of the standard form lease, professional cleaning is only mandatory if it is *required* to restore the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Since you have already achieved this through your own efforts, you are not legally obligated to pay for or provide a receipt from a professional cleaner. If they continue to demand it, you can point them to the specific wording in the current standard form lease and section 27C of the Act.

### What the Law Says About Your Situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, your rental provider is legally obligated to maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). When damage occurs, you are required to notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

Because the burglary damaged your plumbing and wiring, these issues qualify as **urgent repairs** (such as a burst water service or failure of an essential service) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs immediately after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Your Options Before the Lease Ends
1. **Request Urgent Repairs & Claim Reimbursement**: If your rental provider does not arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the plumbing and wiring immediately, you can take reasonable steps to arrange the repairs yourself [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may be reimbursed directly by the provider for the reasonable cost of these urgent repairs, up to **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If the cost exceeds $2500 or the provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
2. **Terminate the Lease Early Without Penalty**: If the damage (e.g., lack of plumbing/wiring) makes the premises "unfit for habitation" or "destroyed," you can give your rental provider a notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). In this specific scenario, the rental provider **cannot** charge you compensation for the remaining rent on your fixed-term lease [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They are also legally required to take all reasonable steps to re-let the premises to minimise any losses [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for Severe Hardship**: If continuing with the tenancy while repairs are pending would cause you severe hardship due to unforeseen circumstances, you can apply to VCAT for an order to reduce the term of your agreement and make necessary variations under section 91U [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Your Ongoing Obligations
* You must keep the premises reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* Regarding cleaning at the end of the tenancy, the provider cannot require you to pay for professional cleaning unless it is strictly necessary to restore the premises to the condition they were in when you moved in (accounting for fair wear and tear) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 is version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't use the phrase "Authorised Version," so these numbers come from the document metadata.

## What the law says

- **Rental minimum standards:** The property must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition at move-in:** The landlord must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp count as urgent:** "Urgent repairs" include "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** Before you move in, the landlord must give you a signed condition report stating the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you aren't given one, you may complete one yourself, and it is taken as notice to the landlord of any defects it records [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You may apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate report within 30 days of the agreement starting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the landlord in writing now.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware" of damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Put the mould, damp and rotting timber in writing and attach photos.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and the landlord cannot be reached or doesn't act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary says reimbursement can be up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for urgent repairs** if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for non-urgent repairs.** If the work isn't urgent, you can apply to the Director after giving written notice and waiting 14 days without repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can then apply to VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord has failed to carry out the repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds rent back. It is not a reduction, and the Tribunal decides whether it applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your three questions

- **Ask for repairs:** Yes, as described above.
- **Lower rent:** The retrieved documents don't contain a provision that reduces rent for disrepair. The closest option is the Rent Special Account in point 5 above.
- **Cancel:** The retrieved documents don't set out a clear right for you to end the agreement over these conditions. Form 2 refers to notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but the text of section 91ZD was not retrieved, so I can't tell you its conditions. Section 80 also says renters can't use the repair remedies where a Housing Act 1983 declaration that the house is unfit for habitation is in force [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell whether that applies to you.

Before deciding whether to end the agreement, check those provisions and get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate. Consumer Affairs also publishes guidance at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Which law applies:** The current *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because the lease started in 2024, the documents don't show whether the 2024 standard form had the same wording.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease may require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the tenancy started, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations say the provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to their move-in condition, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Under the standard form, the renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their move-in condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of a tenancy, a renter must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning from the bond only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Check the condition report.** The standard form requires you to have been given two copies (or one emailed copy) of the condition report on or before you moved in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This is the main benchmark for "move-in condition" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Check whether a professional clean was done before you moved in.** If it was, and you were told so, the provider may have a stronger basis to require one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If not, the regulations limit what can be required [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent in writing** what professional cleaning is said to be required to restore the carpets to move-in condition, and by reference to what. The documents don't set out a procedure for this.
- **If there's a bond claim,** you can dispute it. Bond claim evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If a claim is made without your consent, the Authority must notify you, and you can stop it being paid automatically by notifying the Authority in writing within 14 days that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the term is harsh or unconscionable,** you can apply to VCAT for an order declaring it invalid or varying it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What helps show the carpets' condition**

The documents name the **condition report** as the key reference point [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They don't list other types of evidence. Practical steps not covered by the documents include keeping dated photos or video of the carpets before and after your clean, and keeping your own cleaning receipts or notes.

**What the documents don't answer**

- Whether an agent can insist on a professional-cleaner receipt, or what counts as proof.
- What the 2024 version of the standard form said.
- Whether your own cleaning meets the "restore to move-in condition" test. That depends on facts in your condition report and on fair wear and tear, which the documents don't assess for your case.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For a firm answer, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

- **The renter is not automatically liable for break-in damage.** The renter's duty not to damage the premises covers damage caused intentionally or negligently by the renter or a visitor, and "damage does not include fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the burglars count as visitors (someone on the premises with the renter's permission) is a question the documents don't answer.

2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you have "taken reasonable steps" to get the provider to repair immediately and cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must then give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost, and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Reimbursement is capped at the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations summary gives the prescribed amount as up to $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to reimburse you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends and give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Your lease may not be on that form.

- Whether the burglary is covered by insurance, or whether police reporting affects the renter's rights.
- Whether the provider can claim the cost of damage from the bond.

At least 3 days before a claim is made to the landlord, the landlord or agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Bond claim evidence includes "an invoice," "a receipt," "a quote," or "a photograph" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The claim must match the condition report.** Bond claim evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Signing is a separate step.** A landlord "must not request or obtain a renter's signature to a claim form" unless the form specifies the amount to be refunded and any apportionment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlords can still pursue more money.** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded from taking proceedings under this Part to recover an additional amount by way of compensation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This suggests a landlord may still seek extra money through the Tribunal, but the documents don't set out how a post-bond invoice would be enforced.
- **Professional cleaning limits.** A standard-form term can require a renter to pay for professional cleaning only if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, "taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The landlord also must not require professional cleaning unless the premises were professionally cleaned before the tenancy started, or it's needed to restore the premises to that condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for bond claim evidence.** Request the invoice, quote, receipts, and photos the agent relies on. The Act requires these to be given at least 3 days before a claim is made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your condition report.** Compare the cleaning charge with the condition report from the start of the tenancy, since the cleaning must be measured against that condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether the cleaning was "reasonable."** The Act only allows the "reasonable cost" of cleaning, so ask whether the amount is reasonable and whether it was professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask whether a claim form was ever lodged.** If no form was lodged and your full bond was released, you can ask the agent to explain the basis for the separate charge.
5. **Seek advice or dispute it.** If the agent pursues the amount, the Tribunal handles compensation disputes. I haven't retrieved the full procedure for those applications, so please check that before taking steps.

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether a verbal agreement to a bond deduction counts as agreeing to pay an invoice.
- How a landlord recovers a cleaning invoice after the bond has been fully returned, including the time limits and procedure for that claim.
- Whether the bond was released through a valid claim process in your case.

answer:
## What the law says

I used the Act and Regulations in force today (9 November 2026).

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, dated 13 October 2026. Its metadata gives the version as 115 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't print an "Authorised Version" label, so I'm relying on that metadata.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, dated 30 June 2026, version 009 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**1. A fee-free payment method must be available.**
- The provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than the renter's own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to the renter [1, s 42(4)].
- The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your free bank transfer fits this. Electronic funds transfer is also the prescribed payment method that must be permitted [2, reg 19; 1, s 42(5)].
- The documents don't say whether a "slower" free option is still "reasonably available".

**2. The agent must disclose costs first.**
- Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur. These expressly include third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [1, s 42(7)].

**3. Fees on rent payments are restricted, whoever gets the money.**
- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for establishing or using direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [1, s 51(3)(b)]. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Separately, a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent [1, s 51A]. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed matters include "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". Regulation 21C has applied since 31 March 2026 [2, reg 21C(2)(i)].

## Does it matter if the fee goes to the app company or the agent?

**Mostly no.** Sections 51(3) and 51A apply to "a person", not just the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A fee kept by the payments company is therefore not automatically outside them.

There are two limits:
- The duties in s 42(4) and s 42(7) bind the provider and agent specifically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your agent remains responsible for having a free method available and for disclosing the card fee.
- Section 51A excludes an "ADI" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and reg 21C excludes surcharges "permitted under any other Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents don't define "ADI" or say which other Act permits surcharges. I can't tell you whether your payments company falls into either exception.

## Can the app charge you the card fee?

On these documents, a card fee on rent is likely prohibited unless one of those two exceptions applies. I can't confirm that either does. The documents also don't say whether a card fee counts as an "electronic payment facility" charge under s 51(3).

## What you can do

- **Use the free bank transfer.** That avoids the fee [1, s 42(4)].
- **Ask your agent in writing** to confirm which fee-free method is available and what the card fee is. They must give you this cost information before you consent [1, s 42(7)].
- **Ask for the legal basis of the surcharge.** Ask whether they rely on the ADI exception or on a surcharge permitted under another Act [1; 2].
- **If you've already paid the fee,** the documents don't cover refunds, complaints or VCAT steps, so I can't advise on those from them.

answer:
**Sources:** *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115 per its metadata, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions I retrieved, and they cover today's date. The files do not use the words "Authorised Version No.", so the version numbers come from the metadata.

## What the law says

- **Minimum standards:** The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Damp and structure:** Under the standards, the premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The definition includes a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards. It also includes faults that make the premises unsafe, such as "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease**
- A lease ends if you have not entered into possession and you give the provider a notice of termination on one of these grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - the premises are not in good repair;
  - the premises are unfit for human habitation;
  - the premises do not meet any rental minimum standards; or
  - the premises are for any other reason unavailable for occupation.
- Damp, mould and rotting timber could fit the first three grounds, but whether they do is a question of fact.
- Collecting the keys may or may not count as "entered into possession". The retrieved text does not define the term. Do not move in or store belongings until you have settled this.
- The retrieved text gives no required form or notice period for this notice. Put it in writing and keep a copy.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- You can issue a request for urgent repairs to bring the premises up to the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Give written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the provider does not act immediately, you can arrange urgent repairs yourself. You must first have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form agreement summary states the reimbursement cap as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the provider has not acted within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate or apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order specified repairs by a suitably qualified person, within a set time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Once you have given repair notice, you can ask VCAT to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. VCAT must make the order if the provider has not done the repairs and has not shown financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Lower rent**
- I found no provision in the retrieved documents that lets you simply reduce the rent for damp or mould.
- The rent-free rule in section 65(3) applies only where premises are not vacant or not reasonably clean. It runs from the agreed move-in day until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not extend it to damp or mould.
- Rent accrues from day to day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order compensation under section 212(2) when the provider breaches the repair duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The text of section 212 was not retrieved, so I cannot say how it works.
- The Rent Special Account holds your rent while repairs are outstanding. It is not a reduction [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Also useful:** The provider must give you a condition report before you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Within 30 days of the agreement starting, you can ask VCAT to amend a condition report that is inaccurate or incomplete [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of the defects it records [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Not covered in the retrieved documents
- Whether collecting the keys counts as "entered into possession".
- The form and timing of a notice under the cancellation provision.
- A general right to a rent reduction.

Photograph the defects and put everything in writing.

A broken tap that forced you to shut off water to the whole house probably fits one of these. The documents don't say which category applies to your tap.
- **You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if both of these are true** (s 72(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  1. You've taken reasonable steps to arrange for the rental provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  2. You're unable to get them to carry out the repairs.
- **The repair must be done by a suitably qualified person.** The standard rental agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says this includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So use a licensed plumber.
- **The documents don't address the owner's "own tradespeople only" rule.** Nothing in them says a provider can require that only their chosen tradespeople do urgent repairs, or that this stops you using s 72. The test in s 72 is whether you've taken reasonable steps and can't get the repair done. The documents also don't say whether two calls count as "reasonable steps". That is a judgement on the facts.

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice of the breakdown.** The Act requires a renter to give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of provided facilities or fixtures (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email counts, because the Act allows notices to be given by electronic communication [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a record of both phone calls.
2. **Ask for a firm, immediate time.** If the owner's tradesperson still can't come immediately, you can arrange the repair under s 72(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **After a repair you've arranged** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

   - They must reimburse you within 7 days after receiving that written notice.
4. **Reimbursement limit.** The standard rental agreement summary says a renter may be reimbursed the reasonable cost of repairs up to **$2500** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep your invoice. I didn't retrieve the regulation that sets the prescribed amount itself, so check that if the cost may be near that figure.
5. **If you can't pay, or the owner won't reimburse you,** you can apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):

   - If you've paid, given written notice, and weren't reimbursed within 7 days, you can apply for a compensation or compliance order (s 209AAB) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Also check your paperwork.** If an agent manages the property, the provider must have given you a written statement saying whether the agent can authorise urgent repairs, up to what amount, and the number to call [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). - **Prohibited terms.** A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring all or part of the premises to be professionally cleaned at the end of the tenancy, unless that term is in the standard form. The same applies to a term making the renter pay for professional cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do and ask

1. **Ask the agent for the legal basis.** If the carpets are in their move-in condition, professional cleaning isn't "required to restore" them under clause 11 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can ask the agent to point to the provision they rely on.
2. **Check the "cleaned before you moved in" exception.** Professional cleaning can only be required if it was done before your tenancy and you were told [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Look at your move-in paperwork for that.

The Act also notes the Tribunal may declare terms invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Evidence of the carpets' condition

The prescribed condition report (Form 4) is the key document [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):

- **Move-in condition report.** It lists floor coverings and records whether each item is clean, undamaged and working. It is meant to help resolve disputes over cleaning and damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep your signed copy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own comments and photos.** The form invites you to comment and attach photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos at both ends of the tenancy.** Take them at the beginning and end. They should be dated and labelled, show the location or room, and include close-ups and wider shots [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The final inspection.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy part of the report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a reasonable opportunity to be present, and they must allow for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Leaving early because the premises are unusable.** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe. The termination date can be the day you give the notice or a later date (s 91ZD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ordinary early exit.** A normal notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days' notice (s 91Z) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For a fixed-term lease, a notice with a termination date before the end of the term is of no effect in the ordinary case (s 91ZA(1)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). With about three weeks left, this route doesn't give you anything.
- **Urgent repairs.** The definition covers a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglary damage to plumbing and wiring may fall within these, but that depends on the facts.
- **Reporting damage.** A renter must give written notice of damage to the rental provider as soon as practicable (ss 62, 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can take into account whether you gave that notice when it decides compensation claims (s 211(h)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable", and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Damage duty.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises (s 61) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice of the break-ins and damage now.** Email counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy.
2. **Ask the rental provider (or agent) to carry out urgent repairs immediately.**
   - If they don't, you may arrange the urgent repairs yourself, provided you took reasonable steps to get them done and couldn't (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - The regulations' standard rental agreement summary states the reimbursement limit as $2,500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't reimburse you within 7 days of written notice, you can apply for a compliance or compensation order (s 209AAB, s 212(1B)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give notice of intention to vacate under s 91ZD**, but only if the damage really makes the premises unfit for human habitation or unsafe. You can set the termination date as today or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say what counts as "unfit" or "unsafe", so you would be judging that yourself. A dispute would be for VCAT.
5. **Explain the cleaning problem in writing.** Say you can't clean properly because of the damage. That supports your position under the "as far as practicable" wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say who bears the cost of burglar damage, or how the bond would be treated. Section 61 only refers to damage a renter causes intentionally or negligently [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- They don't say whether this particular damage meets the "unfit" or "unsafe" test.
- They don't address insurance or police reports.

For a firm answer on those points, get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre. The Act's urgent-repairs and VCAT provisions are time-sensitive, so act quickly.

## What the law says

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026** says the rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from the renter’s own bank or account fees—is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act also prohibits a person other than an **ADI** from demanding or receiving a fee for a prescribed matter relating to payment of rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The current **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, prescribe **“rent payment”** as such a matter, except for payment-surcharge fees permitted under another Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act separately prohibits charges for establishing or using a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) It also requires the rental provider or agent to tell the renter, before the renter consents to a payment method, about costs including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Therefore:

- **The card fee is not automatically lawful merely because the payments company—not the agent—charges it.** The prohibition applies to “a person other than an ADI,” and the retrieved documents do not say whether this particular payments company is an ADI. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **The fee may be covered by the prohibition** if it is a fee for rent payment or use of an electronic payment facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- **The documents do not establish that a card surcharge is permitted under another Act**, so they do not provide enough information to confirm that exception applies. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- A no-fee manual bank-transfer option may satisfy the fee-free-method requirement, but the documents do not define when a method is “reasonably available” or say whether being slower makes this option unreasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must permit electronic funds transfer as a prescribed payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can ask or do

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. Whether the payments company is an **ADI**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. What legal authority under another Act is relied on for the card surcharge, if any. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. Why the no-fee bank-transfer method is considered reasonably available despite being slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
4. For the required information about all costs, including third-party transaction fees, before consenting to use the card method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the documents provided, you can plainly say that **it is not established that the card fee is lawful**, and that directing the fee through the payments company does not, by itself, answer the issue. The documents do not state who is legally responsible where a third-party payments company imposes the fee, so that specific point cannot be answered more definitively from them.

## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026, Author: Barbara Hargreaves** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, Author: Lavina Mandy** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The premises must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Rotting timber, damp and structural mould may therefore indicate breaches of the rental provider’s duties, depending on the facts and extent of the damage. The documents do not specifically classify rotting timber as an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing immediately.**  
   Describe each problem, attach dated photographs or reports, and ask the provider to confirm whether the premises comply with the minimum standards and when qualified tradespeople will repair them. The prescribed condition-report form says defects and needed repairs should be recorded and reported to the provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs before moving in.**  
   For non-urgent repairs, if the provider does not repair the premises within **14 days** after receiving written notice, you may apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs; the Tribunal must hear that application within **7 days**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal may order repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not arrange major repairs yourself without advice.**  
   The Act allows a renter to arrange urgent repairs only after taking reasonable steps to have the provider arrange them immediately and being unable to get the provider to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that these particular problems are urgent repairs, so the safer documented route is written notice and an application for orders.

4. **Ask to end the agreement by mutual agreement.**  
   You can ask the provider to agree in writing to cancel the agreement and refund any bond or rent paid. The documents do not state a general right to cancel merely because the renter discovers damp, mould or rotting timber before moving in. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **Consider statutory termination only if the premises are unfit for habitation.**  
   The prescribed agreement refers to a renter giving notice under section 91ZD where the premises are “destroyed or unfit for habitation”; in that situation the provider is not entitled to compensation for rent foregone under the agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not provide the full test or procedure for deciding whether this house is legally unfit for habitation, so they do not establish that you can use that provision on these facts.

6. **Ask for a lower rent, but it is not an automatic entitlement shown here.**  
   You may negotiate a rent reduction, particularly until the repairs are completed. The documents do not provide a general right to unilaterally reduce the rent because of these defects. Instead, after giving repair notice and if the provider fails to comply, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order allowing rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account**, subject to the statutory conditions; this is not the same as simply withholding or reducing rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Practical bottom line:** document everything, notify the provider in writing, request either prompt repairs or written agreement to end the lease, and do not simply stop paying rent. - Plumbing or electrical damage may require **urgent repairs**. The regulations expressly refer to urgent repairs involving a burst water service or flood damage, and say urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service supplied by the rental provider. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If the premises are **unfit for human habitation** or have been destroyed or rendered unsafe, you may give a notice of intention to vacate that takes effect **on the date it is given or a later date**, even though the lease is fixed-term. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The ordinary notice to vacate does not generally end a fixed-term agreement early: it is ineffective if it specifies a date before the fixed term ends. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises reasonably clean **“as far as practicable”**, and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed agreement also says the renter is not required to arrange professional cleaning unless the specified statutory conditions apply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Immediately send written notice** to the rental provider or agent describing the break-ins and each plumbing, wiring, security and safety problem. Keep copies, photographs and any repair reports. The Act permits electronic notice in accordance with the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

- A bond claim must use an Authority-approved form. If the provider claims without everyone’s consent, the Authority must notify the other parties, who have **14 days** to notify the Authority that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Before making a claim for payment to the provider, the provider must give the renter supporting **bond claim evidence** at least **3 days** beforehand; an invoice is one type of bond claim evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- The Act does say that the Tribunal can award compensation where a party failed to comply with the rental agreement or the Act, and that the Tribunal may consider whether the renter consented to the failure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**Therefore:** agreeing that an amount could be taken from the bond is not, on the documents provided, clearly the same thing as agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Your actual words, the amount agreed, the cleaning condition, the condition reports and the invoice would matter.

You can ask the agent to provide:

1. the signed or written agreement showing exactly what amount and liability you accepted;
2. the condition report and final inspection report;
3. the cleaning invoice, receipt or other evidence of the actual cost; and
4. an explanation why the full bond was returned and why a separate invoice was issued later.

You can dispute the invoice in writing and say that you agreed only to a bond deduction—not necessarily to a separate payment—and that the full bond was later repaid. Ask them to identify the legal or contractual basis for the invoice and to show that the cost is reasonable and relates to cleaning required under the Act. * **A fee-free method must be available:** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This means external payment apps or processors can charge you, provided the fee complies with other applicable laws (such as credit card surcharging regulations).
* **Upfront disclosure is mandatory:** Before you agree to use a specific payment method, the provider or agent must give you clear information about any costs you will incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **You cannot be forced into a paid option:** The tenancy agreement cannot contain a term that requires you to pay rent via a method that incurs additional costs (other than your own bank fees) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, general `"rent payment"` fees are prohibited unless they qualify as legitimate surcharge fees permitted under another Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

1. **Confirm the fee is a legitimate surcharge:** Ensure the charge is a standard credit/debit card processing fee allowed under financial regulations, rather than an illegal administrative `"rent payment"` fee [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

If they cannot prove this was done, they are legally required to provide it now.
3. **Continue using the free option:** You are fully within your rights to stick with the manual bank transfer. The law guarantees that a fee-free method must remain reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Who receives the fee is irrelevant:** It does not matter whether the money goes to the payments app company or the agent. The law treats `"third party transaction fees"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and agent-collected fees under the exact same disclosure rules, as long as a fee-free alternative exists and you are informed upfront.

### What the law says about your situation
Your landlord has strict legal obligations regarding the condition of the property before you move in. Under the rental minimum standards, each room in the premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The premises must also be structurally sound and weatherproof [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber likely breaches this structural standard. Your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises comply with these minimum standards and are in a fit condition for occupation when you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
**1. Ask for repairs: Yes.**
Damp or mould caused by the building structure is legally classified as an "urgent repair" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You should notify your landlord in writing immediately. If they fail to act, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them to carry out the urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). For non-urgent structural issues (like rotting timber that isn't making the property unsafe), you must give written notice and wait 14 days before applying to VCAT for a compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If VCAT finds your landlord in breach, they can order the repairs to be done by a qualified person and may also order compensation under section 212(2) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for lower rent: Not directly, but you can control payments.**
The provided documents do not explicitly grant a right to unilaterally "lower" or reduce your rent. An owner's internal policy restricting repairs to their own tradespeople does not override this statutory right when they are unresponsive [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 4. **If Costs Exceed $2,500 or You Cannot Pay Upfront:** If the repair costs more than the cap or you cannot afford it, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner to carry out the repairs directly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v115)**, which is in force today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation and what you can do:

### What the law says about your situation
Under Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider has a duty to ensure rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If burglary damage to plumbing and wiring makes the property unsafe or impossible to live in, the Act provides specific legal pathways for early lease termination and emergency repairs. 

### What you can do or ask for

**1. Report the damage immediately**
The law requires you to give written notice to your rental provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of any damage to the premises or breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your notice must clearly state both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature (e.g., broken plumbing and wiring) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Arrange urgent repairs yourself (or apply to the Tribunal)**
If the damaged plumbing or wiring constitutes an "urgent repair" (such as a serious fault making the premises unsafe, unsecure, or uninhabitable), you can arrange for the repairs to be done if your provider won't do it immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* If you pay for these urgent repairs yourself, you must give your provider written notice of the work and costs within 7 days, and they are legally required to reimburse you for the reasonable costs within 7 days of receiving that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* If you cannot afford the repairs or the cost exceeds the prescribed limit, you can apply directly to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider to do the work. The Tribunal must hear this application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Give a Notice of Intention to Vacate (if the property is unsafe/uninhabitable)**
If the burglary damage has rendered the premises "unfit for human habitation" or destroyed them "to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe," you are entitled to give your provider a notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* You can specify a termination date that is **the same day you give the notice** or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This allows you to end the fixed-term lease early without penalty if the property is genuinely uninhabitable.

**4. Apply to the Tribunal for termination due to severe hardship**
If the situation does not quite meet the threshold for being "unfit for habitation" but still causes you significant distress, you can apply to the Tribunal under the "hardship" provisions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* The Tribunal may order to reduce your fixed-term lease or terminate it entirely if they are satisfied that an unforeseen change in your circumstances would cause you **severe hardship** that is greater than the hardship your provider would suffer by ending the lease early [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Recommended next steps
1. Send a written notice to your agent/provider detailing the burglary damage and requesting urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. If they do not act immediately, get quotes for urgent repairs and proceed if necessary, keeping all receipts for reimbursement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

A renter may give notice to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been destroyed to an extent that makes them unsafe. Your free bank transfer may satisfy this. The Act doesn't say whether a slower method still counts as "reasonably available", so I can't say.

They must do this before you consent to that method (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Some charges are banned outright.** A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter for the first issue of a rent payment card. Nor can they charge for the establishment or use of direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 51(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent payment fees can be banned by regulation.** A person, other than an ADI (authorised deposit-taking institution, i.e. a bank-type lender), must not demand or receive a fee for any "prescribed matter" in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who receives the fee?

Version 115 says only "a person, other than an ADI", and notes that s 51A was substituted by No. 46/2025 s 13 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the app company is an ADI, s 51A would not apply to it. Section 51(3), as printed, has no ADI exception [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7) bind only the provider and the agent.** They don't bind the app company directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They still apply to your agent, because the agent chose the app.
