I can't confirm either way.
- **Remedies.** The documents I retrieved don't cover refunds or complaint processes.

1. **Ask your agent in writing** to confirm the fee-free method that is reasonably available to you. Ask them also to disclose all the app's fees (s 42(4), (7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use the free bank transfer** to avoid the card fee. It is slower, so pay early.
3. **Query the card fee itself.** Ask the agent or the app company to explain why it is lawful given ss 51(3) and 51A, and ask for it to be removed or refunded if they can't. Whether it must be removed turns on the unresolved point above.

- **Day of occupation.** The provider must make sure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed day. Document the problems with photos and the condition report, and send your notice in writing. Check with VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria before you give any notice to end the lease.

## What the law says

I used the versions in force today (9 November 2026):
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**You don't have to wait indefinitely.** Under section 72 of the Act, a renter may arrange urgent repairs if both of these are true [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
1. You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider (or their agent) to carry out the repairs immediately.
2. You are unable to get them to carry out the repairs.

The regulations' standard form says the same. It also says the rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the provider or agent in writing now.** You must give written notice as soon as practicable of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures the provider supplied [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Written notice also helps show you took "reasonable steps".
2. **If they still can't act, arrange the repair yourself.** The regulations say only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Use a qualified tradesperson rather than doing it yourself.
3. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim reimbursement.** The provider is liable for the reasonable cost, or any greater prescribed amount, whichever is less. This includes GST, and they must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' form summary says reimbursement is up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Go to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an order requiring the urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The form states that amount as $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- **"Owner only uses their own tradespeople."** Nothing I retrieved says a provider can limit repairs to their own tradespeople. Section 72 turns on whether you took reasonable steps and couldn't get the repair done [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether two calls in one day, with the provider saying no one is available yet, is enough. I can't say how a tribunal would see that.

answer:
## What the law says

**Document and version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 October 2026), is the latest version I retrieved. It has no end date, so I treat it as the one in force today [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- A residential rental agreement must not include a term requiring professional cleaning, or requiring the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard form can only carry a prescribed term. That term applies if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, taking fair wear and tear into account [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Regulations:** The prescribed wording is in regulation 12 of the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*. The provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless one of two things applies:
- (a) Professional cleaning was done immediately before the tenancy started, and the renter was told so.
- (b) Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, "having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The standard form repeats this in its professional cleaning clause [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Its pet clause only says the renter must get consent and that the provider must not unreasonably refuse [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It says nothing about carpet cleaning.

**Caveat on the Regulations:** The retrieved versions are v002 (1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and v004 (1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve a version in force today. Regulation 12 reads the same in both. I can't confirm the current wording from these documents. Also, my second search failed, so I did not look for anything beyond these.

**What this means for you:** Your pet clause is an additional term, not part of the standard form. As you describe it, a blanket "professionally clean the carpets" requirement looks like a prohibited term, and so would be void and unenforceable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I haven't seen your exact wording, so check it. Even without that, the standard-form test is about condition, not receipts. If the carpets are back to their starting condition, professional cleaning isn't "required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

One exception to check: if the premises were professionally cleaned just before you moved in and you were told, the provider can require professional cleaning (a) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- **Put it in writing.** Tell the agent that the carpets are in the same condition as at move-in, and that under regulation 12 and section 27B a receipt can't be demanded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge the term.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to have a term declared invalid or varied if it is harsh or unconscionable [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What helps show the carpets' condition

The condition report form (Form 4) says:
- **Keep your copy.** It helps resolve cleaning disputes at the end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Take photos.** They should be taken at the beginning and at the end of the tenancy, be dated and labelled, show the room, and include close-ups and wider shots [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your move-in comments and photos.** Floor coverings are an item the condition report lists [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). **Short answer:** If the burglary damage makes the premises unfit to live in or unsafe, you can give notice and leave early without waiting for the lease to end. Whether the damage reaches that level is a factual question the documents can't settle.

**Which version I used.** The version in force today (9 November 2026) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve any later versions.

## What the law says

- **Leaving early because of the condition of the premises (s 91ZD).** A renter may give the rental provider a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or to such an extent as to be rendered unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing.** The notice can give the day you send it, or a later date, as the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That means no 28-day wait.
- **Why the usual route doesn't fit.** In a fixed-term lease, an ordinary notice that ends the lease before the term ends is of no effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The usual notice period is 28 days. That wording is not in the v115 excerpt. It appears in earlier versions, such as Version 110 (6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Either way, with about three weeks left, s 91ZD is the relevant route.
- **Lease break fees.** The regulations' form for agreements of more than 5 years says no "rent foregone" is payable if the renter ends the agreement under s 91ZD [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I did not find the equivalent clause for the standard form. Check your own agreement.

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Report the damage in writing now.** The regulations' summary of renter duties says a renter must notify the rental provider in writing when damage occurs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act's own duty is s 72AA, but I only found it in Version 111 (25 November 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Include the plumbing and wiring damage and the break-ins.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The summary says urgent repairs include failure of essential services. The rental provider must carry them out after being notified [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You may arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the provider to act and they haven't. You can then be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do the repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - The Act's sections on this (ss 72–73) appear in the documents only in Version 111 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), which is not the current version. I couldn't confirm the wording in Version 115.
3. **Consider a s 91ZD notice** if the premises are genuinely unfit or unsafe, for example because the plumbing and wiring faults make them uninhabitable. You could give it for the day you send it or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** You can apply to VCAT if the provider hasn't done them within 14 days of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The documents don't say who is liable for burglary damage, or what happens to your bond.

The regulations' form says a renter must keep the premises reasonably clean and pay for professional cleaning only if it is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- I found no mention of insurance or police reports.

- **Safeguards on the form.** The provider must not request or obtain your signature on a claim form that doesn't state the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned. - **Evidence.** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment of bond to the provider is made, the provider or agent must give each renter bond claim evidence. That evidence must not conflict with a statement in a condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say. They only set out the bond-claim process above. ## What the law says

The current documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The premises must comply with rental minimum standards. They must be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and each room must be free from **mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The standard agreement states that the agreement’s start date is the date from which the renter may move in. It also says the rental provider must provide premises complying with the minimum standards, vacant and reasonably clean, when the renter moves in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The documents do **not** say that collecting the keys or not yet moving in automatically cancels the agreement.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the rental provider in writing immediately.** Describe the damp, mould and rotting timber, attach dated photographs or other evidence, and state that the defects appear inconsistent with the structural-soundness, weatherproofing and mould/damp standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) The renter must give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of supplied facilities, fixtures, furniture or equipment. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for the defects to be repaired before you move in**, and ask for written confirmation of the repair scope and completion date. Non-urgent repairs must be carried out in a reasonable time; after written notice, you may apply to VCAT if they have not been done within **14 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT can order specified repairs, require a suitably qualified person to do them, and order compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **If the condition makes the premises unsafe or uninhabitable, ask urgently for action.** The retrieved documents do not provide enough information to classify damp, mould and rotting timber in a residential house as an “urgent repair” on those facts alone. They do state that urgent repairs must be carried out after notice, and that VCAT applications for urgent repairs may be made where the renter cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

4. **You can ask the provider to agree to cancel the lease without penalty**, or to agree in writing to a reduced rent while specified repairs are outstanding. However, the retrieved documents do not state a general right to cancel in this situation, nor do they state a specific statutory right to a rent reduction merely because the renter has not yet moved in. Do not simply stop paying rent or treat the lease as cancelled without an agreement or an order.

5. **If repairs are not done, consider the formal repair remedies.** You may apply to the Director to investigate after giving written notice and waiting 14 days; the Director may negotiate repairs or issue a report directing the provider to comply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You may also apply to VCAT for non-urgent repairs after the 14-day period. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also allows a renter who has given a repair notice to seek an order permitting rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account** if the provider has failed to repair, subject to the statutory conditions; this is not the same as an automatic rent reduction. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Preserve the keys, lease, inspection records, photographs, messages and any reports. The retrieved documents do not contain a specific cancellation procedure for your precise pre-move-in situation, so they do not establish that you can unilaterally terminate without possible liability.

The retrieved provisions do **not** say that:

- agreeing that cleaning may be deducted from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a later, separate invoice;
- failing to sign a bond claim form automatically cancels any separate agreement;
- receiving the whole bond automatically extinguishes, or confirms, a separate cleaning debt; or
- a separate invoice is enforceable in these circumstances.

So, **the documents do not establish that you must pay the invoice**. They also do not establish that you definitely do not have to pay it. Whether your agreement created a separate obligation would depend on the terms and evidence of that agreement, which the retrieved documents do not address.

You can ask the agent to identify:

1. the legal or contractual basis for the invoice;
2. whether they are relying on your agreement to a **bond deduction** or claiming a separate debt; and
3. the evidence supporting the claimed cleaning cost.

You can state that you did not sign a bond claim form, that the full bond was repaid, and that you do not accept that an agreement about a bond deduction was necessarily an agreement to pay a separate invoice. The Act permits a provider to claim cleaning costs from the bond, but the retrieved provisions do not explain how that bond process determines liability for a later invoice. Here is how the law applies to your situation:

**1. Can the app charge you a card fee?**
Yes, a third-party payments company can legally charge a fee for processing your rent by card. However, this is only permitted if your rental provider or agent also provides a reasonably available payment method that incurs **no additional costs** (other than standard bank or account fees on your own banking app) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The current regulations explicitly note in the standard tenancy agreement that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method and allow you to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

**2. Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?**
No, it does not matter who collects the fee. The law places the obligation on the rental provider or their agent to ensure a fee-free option is available, regardless of who charges for the alternative card payment service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, before you consent to use any payment method that has a cost, the provider or agent must give you clear information about those costs upfront. The law explicitly defines these costs to include **"third party transaction fees"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 

**What you can do:**
* **Use the fee-free option:** Since your agent offers a manual bank transfer with no fee, you are fully entitled to use this method without penalty or delay from the provider. 
* **Check your agreement:** Review your standard tenancy agreement (under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*) to confirm the listed payment methods [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
* **Report non-compliance:** If your agent refuses to accept the fee-free bank transfer, penalizes you for using it, or fails to disclose third-party fees upfront, they are breaching their obligations under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version rta-1997-v111) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### 1. Notify Your Provider Immediately
You must notify your rental provider in writing about the damage to the premises as soon as possible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

### 2. Pursue Urgent Repairs
The damaged plumbing and wiring likely qualify as **urgent repairs** (such as a burst water service, gas leak, or flood damage) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your provider is legally required to carry out these repairs immediately after you notify them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **If they refuse or delay:** You can arrange for a suitably qualified person to fix the issue yourself and claim reimbursement from your provider for reasonable costs up to **$2,500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Terminate the Lease Early (Unfit for Habitation)
Because the damage is severe enough that you cannot even clean properly, the premises may be legally considered **"unfit for habitation."** 
* You can give notice under section 91ZD of the Act to end your fixed-term lease early [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Crucial Protection:** If you terminate on this basis, your rental provider **cannot** claim compensation for the remaining three weeks of rent (known as "rent foregone") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Apply to VCAT
If your rental provider refuses to address the urgent repairs or fails to act within a reasonable timeframe, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring them to carry out the necessary work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

**Recommended Next Step:** Send a written notice to your provider immediately detailing the damage, classifying it as an urgent repair, and stating that if the premises are deemed unfit for habitation, you reserve the right to terminate the agreement under section 91ZD without liability for the remaining rent.

Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)**, which is in force today (from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

**Do you have to pay the invoice?**
Not automatically. Because your full bond was already returned to you, the statutory process for claiming money from the bond is closed. The agent cannot retroactively take money from your bond without a signed claim form or a Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) order. Whether you owe the invoice depends entirely on whether you actually left the premises unreasonably dirty (excluding fair wear and tear). If you did, they could theoretically pursue it as a separate debt, but sending an invoice does not automatically make it payable.

**Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
No. They are legally distinct:
* A **bond deduction** is a claim against the security deposit held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority. It requires specific statutory procedures and must be submitted on an Authority-approved form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* An **invoice** is a direct request for payment for services rendered. Agreeing to let money be taken from your bond does not legally equate to agreeing to pay a separate invoice, particularly after the bond has already been fully repaid.

**What the law says about cleaning claims**
Under current Victorian tenancy law, a rental provider is only entitled to claim cleaning costs if two conditions are met:
1. The premises were **not left reasonably clean** by you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. The cost claimed is **reasonable** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

The law explicitly considers "fair wear and tear" and the condition of the property when you moved in. You cannot be charged for cleaning just to make the property "spotless" or to a professional standard unless it was genuinely necessary to restore it to its original condition, and even then, only the reasonable cost can be claimed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do:**
* Review your initial condition report and take photos of the property when you moved out. If it was left reasonably clean (accounting for fair wear and tear), you have no obligation to pay the invoice.
* Reply to the agent in writing stating that you do not accept liability for the cleaning costs because the premises were left reasonably clean, and note that the bond process is already closed since the full refund was issued.
* If they continue to demand payment or threaten your rental history, you can seek free advice from the Victorian Tenants Union or apply to VCAT to have the dispute formally resolved.

## What the law says

- **The landlord must maintain the home.** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in, and must maintain them in good repair and a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The standards require the home to be structurally sound and weatherproof, and each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Mould, damp and structural faults can be urgent repairs.** "Urgent repairs" includes any fault or damage that makes premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure, and any failure to comply with rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether the rotting timber is an urgent repair will depend on whether it makes the home unsafe or insecure. The documents don't say how to classify it.
- **Condition report.** Before you move in, the provider must give you a signed condition report stating the state of repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you're given a report, you can record disagreement with any statement, and a report you return is taken as notice to the provider of any defects it states [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Within 30 days after the agreement starts, either party can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete statement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A signed report is conclusive evidence of the condition on the day specified, except for matters you dispute in writing or that couldn't reasonably have been discovered on inspection [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your options

1. **Give written notice now.** You must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Write to them listing the mould, damp and timber problems.
2. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself (if they are urgent).** You may do this if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and they can't or don't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days, up to the lesser of that cost or the prescribed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed amount is summarised as up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT for an urgent repairs order.** You can do this if you can't meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** Give written notice that repairs are needed. If the provider doesn't carry them out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or to VCAT for an order requiring repairs. VCAT must hear that application within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Pay rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving a repair notice, you can ask VCAT to order that rent be paid into the Rent Special Account if the provider fails to carry out repairs and cannot show financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This holds your rent. It does not reduce it.

The retrieved documents do not contain a provision that lets you reduce rent for these defects. - I found no provision giving a general right to reduce rent for these defects.

  - If the provider has been given notice of the repairs and hasn't done them, VCAT can authorise you to pay rent into the Rent Special Account. It must do so unless the provider shows financial hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - VCAT can order compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If premises aren't vacant and reasonably clean, rent isn't payable until you move in (see above) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Practical step
Put everything in writing to the provider or agent, with photos. A condition report you give the provider is taken to be notice of the defects it lists [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you weren't given one, you can complete and return your own [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Sources:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Both are the latest versions I retrieved, so they apply today (9 November 2026). The excerpts don't print an "Authorised Version No." label, so the numbers come from the file metadata.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs include water problems.** The definition covers a burst water service, a failure or breakdown of the water supply to rented premises, and a water fitting or fixture malfunctioning so that a substantial amount of water is or will be wasted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A broken tap isn't named, so whether yours qualifies depends on these categories. Having to shut off water to the whole house suggests it does, but that is my reading.
- **When you may arrange the repair.** You may arrange urgent repairs if both of these apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - You have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately.
  - You are unable to get them to do so.
- **Gap in the documents.** They don't define "reasonable steps" or say whether a provider's "own tradespeople only" policy counts as being "unable to get" them to act. Two calls with no repair date is a strong position, but it isn't guaranteed.
- **The repairer must be qualified.** The standard rental agreement says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or not [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). "Suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So hire a licensed plumber rather than doing it yourself.
- **Reimbursement.**
  - The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost, or the prescribed amount if that is less. They must pay within 7 days of receiving your written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The standard agreement summary gives the figure as up to $2500 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Put it in writing now.** Send the provider or agent written notice of the broken tap. You must report damage or breakdowns in writing as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed if electronic service is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Say you've called twice today, that the water is off, and that you'll arrange a licensed plumber if no one can attend immediately. Phone calls alone won't meet the written-notice requirement.
2. **Allow a short, reasonable window** for a response, because the right depends on you having taken reasonable steps first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If there's no workable response, engage a licensed plumber.** Keep the invoice.
4. **Give the provider written notice of the repair and its cost** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse you within 7 days of getting that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If you're not reimbursed within 7 days,** you can apply to VCAT for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If you can't afford the repair, it costs more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay,** you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. VCAT must hear that application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The Act extracts I retrieved don't show an "Authorised Version No." heading, so I'm taking "115" from the file name and metadata. I applied these versions because they are current today. The documents don't include the versions in force when your 2024 lease started.

- **Professional cleaning terms are generally banned.** A lease must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy, or require the renter to pay for it, unless that term is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form allows it only in two cases.** The rental provider must not require professional cleaning unless one of these applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
  1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before your tenancy started and you were told so.
  2. Professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy. This is judged by the condition report, allowing for fair wear and tear.
- **Prohibited terms are void.** A prohibited term in a lease is void and unenforceable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your general duty is lighter.** At the end of the lease you must leave the premises reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Applied to you:** The pet clause is an extra term. On my reading, it can only be enforced to the extent it matches the two standard-form cases above. If your carpets are back to their move-in condition, professional cleaning isn't "required to restore" them, so case 2 shouldn't apply. The documents don't address pet-specific cleaning clauses or receipts, so that is my reading of the general rules rather than something they state directly. The pet provisions I retrieved (ss 71A–71E) say nothing about cleaning conditions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**One thing to check:** Case 1 could apply if the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Look at your condition report and the move-in paperwork.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent which standard-form ground they rely on.** They need either pre-tenancy professional cleaning that you were told about, or a condition-report basis showing it's needed to restore the carpets [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Rely on the condition report.** It is the reference point [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The form says the report "will help to resolve disputes over cleaning" and lists "floor coverings" among the items to be recorded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You should have signed and returned your copy within 5 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Use photos.** The form says to take photos at the beginning and end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They should be dated, labelled and show the location, both close-up and from a distance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Photos of the carpets now, set against your move-in photos and comments, are your best evidence.
4. **Attend the final inspection.** The agent must complete the end-of-tenancy report within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a chance to attend if possible and must allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

# Options for a rental broken into with three weeks left on a fixed term

I used the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026, version 009 per its file name and metadata) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the latest versions in the documents I retrieved. The documents don't confirm that nothing newer exists.

## What the law says

- **Early exit for unfit premises:** A renter may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation, or have been destroyed totally or enough to be unsafe (s 91ZD). The notice can give a termination date that is the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Normal exit rules don't suit you:** An ordinary notice of intention to vacate needs a termination date at least 28 days after the notice is given (s 91Z) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A notice on a fixed-term agreement is also of no effect if its termination date is earlier than the end of the term (s 91ZA(1)(b)). So the ordinary route doesn't help with three weeks left [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include a burst water service, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** At the end of the agreement, a renter must leave the premises reasonably clean "as far as practicable" (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance:** The rental provider must maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Report the damage in writing now.** Renters must give written notice of damage as soon as practicable (s 72AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the provider or agent won't carry out the repairs, you may arrange them yourselves, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately (s 72). You must then give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must reimburse you within 7 days of that notice, up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider ending the lease early under s 91ZD.** This depends on whether the premises are actually unfit for habitation or unsafe. That is a factual question the documents don't decide for your property. The notice must be in writing and signed (s 91ZZN) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agreement ends when you vacate on or after the termination date in the notice (s 91E) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Lease-break costs.** One prescribed form of agreement in the regulations says the provider isn't entitled to "rent foregone" if the renter ends the agreement under s 91ZD [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't tell from the excerpt which form applies to your lease, so check your own agreement.
6. **Hardship.** VCAT can reduce or terminate a fixed term for severe hardship caused by an unforeseen change in circumstances (s 91U) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That seems a weaker fit here than s 91ZD.

## What the documents don't answer

- They don't say who bears the cost of burglary damage, or how your bond or any compensation claim would be treated.
- They don't define "unfit for human habitation".
- They don't cover insurance or police reporting.

You may want to get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

If your tenancy ended long before this version took effect, an earlier version might apply, and the documents don't cover that.

## What the law says

- **Bond claims have a set process.** A claim to the Bond Authority "must be in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A provider can't request or obtain a renter's signature on a claim form unless it states the amount of bond to be refunded and how it is apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning is a valid bond claim.** A provider may claim "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises "reasonably clean" and in the same condition as at the start, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence for bond claims.** At least 3 days before a claim to the bond is made, the provider or agent must give you "bond claim evidence". That means an invoice, receipt, quote, photograph or other prescribed evidence, and it must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A bond claim doesn't stop a further claim.** Someone who has recovered compensation from a bond "is not precluded" from taking Tribunal proceedings to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent can therefore still pursue you, but the route the Act describes is the Tribunal. Under s 212(2) the Tribunal can order compensation if it is satisfied it should be paid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). When it assesses compensation it considers whether money has already been recovered from the bond and whether the applicant mitigated its loss [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A signed condition report is strong evidence.** If both parties signed it, it is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition on the day it states. This doesn't apply to statements you disagreed with in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?

The retrieved text doesn't say so. It doesn't make an informal agreement to a bond deduction into an agreement to pay a separate invoice, and it doesn't make an invoice enforceable on its own. It only provides a formal bond claim (on the approved form) and Tribunal applications [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents say nothing on whether your verbal or informal agreement creates a separate debt under general contract law, so I can't answer that part.

## Do you have to pay?

Not automatically, on what the documents show. Whether you owe anything depends on whether the premises were left reasonably clean compared with the start of the tenancy, and whether the amount is a reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An invoice alone isn't a Tribunal order.

## What you can do

1. **Ask in writing** for the agent's evidence: itemised invoice, photos and the condition report. Compare these with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Dispute the amount in writing** if the premises were reasonably clean or the cost seems unreasonable.
3. **Keep your records**, including the condition reports, any messages where the deduction was discussed, and your bond refund confirmation.
4. **If the agent applies to the Tribunal**, raise the points above, including that the full bond was returned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't give any time limit for the agent to pursue you after the bond is refunded, so I can't say whether one applies.

## What the law says

A failure or breakdown of the **water supply to rented premises** is an urgent repair. A malfunctioning water-using fixture that causes substantial water wastage is also an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Turning off the water to the whole house because of the broken tap appears to fall within those categories, although the documents do not decide the facts of your particular tap. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

You do **not necessarily have to wait for the owner’s preferred tradespeople**. Under section 72 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, a renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider or agent to arrange them immediately, but cannot get them to do so. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations’ standard agreement also says that only a **suitably qualified person** may carry out repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

You can arrange the repair yourself now, provided you use a suitably qualified tradesperson and keep evidence of your two calls and the repair cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act requires you to give the rental provider **7 days’ written notice** of the repair and its cost. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must reimburse the **reasonable cost**, up to **$2,500**, and must pay within **7 days** after receiving your written notice of the repair and cost. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If you cannot pay upfront, the repair costs more than **$2,500**, or the rental provider refuses to pay, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair; VCAT must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if your carpets are reasonably clean and restored to their starting condition, allowing for fair wear and tear, the documents do **not** establish that you must pay for professional cleaning or provide a professional cleaner’s receipt. The documents also do not specifically say that an agent may require a receipt simply because the clause mentions professional cleaning. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The current **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version v115 (13 October 2026)** says a term requiring professional cleaning is prohibited unless it is in the standard form, but confirms that a standard-form agreement may include the prescribed, limited professional-cleaning term. ## What the law says

A renter must leave the premises reasonably clean, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost of cleaning** if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start of the tenancy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A bond claim must be made in an Authority-approved form. If the provider claims repayment of bond, they must give the renter supporting bond-claim evidence at least **3 days beforehand**; an invoice is listed as one type of bond-claim evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act also provides for claims made by the renter, provider, or jointly, and for notice to other parties where the claim is not consented to. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does **not** say in the retrieved provisions that an agreement to deduct cleaning from the bond is automatically an agreement to pay a separate invoice. Nor do the documents say that the absence of your signature on a bond claim form, or the later repayment of the full bond, automatically decides whether you owe the cleaning cost.

The Act does, however, say that recovering compensation from a bond does not prevent a person from bringing proceedings for an **additional** amount of compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) That provision concerns additional compensation; it does not itself establish that every unpaid or separately invoiced cleaning amount is payable.

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent to identify the legal and factual basis for the invoice, including:

- what cleaning was allegedly required;
- why it was more than fair wear and tear;
- the condition report evidence;
- the cleaning invoice or receipt; and

### 📜 What the Law Says
Under the ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997*** (Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf):
* **A fee-free option must be available:** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **Costs must be disclosed upfront:** Before you consent to use a payment method, the provider or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* **You cannot be forced into a costly method:** Your tenancy agreement cannot include a term that requires you to pay rent via a method that incurs additional costs (other than your own bank fees) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Rent payment fees are generally prohibited:** The regulations explicitly list "rent payment" fees as prohibited, with a specific carve-out for *"payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act"* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 💳 Can the app charge you the card fee?
**Yes, but only if strict legal conditions are met.** Because the regulations allow an exception for *"payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act"* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), a third-party payments company may legally charge a card processing surcharge *if* that surcharge is permitted by relevant payment laws. However, this is entirely conditional on:
1. The provider/agent offering you a genuinely fee-free alternative (like the manual bank transfer you mentioned) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. The provider/agent clearly disclosing the exact cost of using the card option **before** you agree to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
**No, it does not matter who ultimately receives the money.** The legal obligation sits squarely with the **residential rental provider or their agent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They are responsible for ensuring that:
* A compliant, fee-free payment method is available.
* You are fully informed of any third-party transaction fees before consenting to use them.

Whether the fee is passed on to a payments processor or kept by the agency does not change their responsibility to provide you with a free alternative and full transparency [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### ✅ What You Can Do or Ask
* **Ask for written confirmation:** Request that your agent confirms in writing that they are providing a compliant, fee-free payment method as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Direct Answer
**No, you do not automatically have to pay the invoice, and agreeing to a bond deduction is not the same as agreeing to pay an invoice.** Under Victorian tenancy law, these are two entirely separate legal mechanisms. 

### Why They Are Different
1. **The Bond Process:** A bond is held by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA), not the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). To access any part of it, the agent must follow a strict statutory process and submit a claim using an approved form to the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because your full bond was returned to you, the agent failed to successfully lodge or sign the required bond claim form in time. Once the bond is paid out, those funds are gone, and the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from it.
2. **The Invoice (Debt) Process:** An invoice is a request for you to pay a debt under your tenancy agreement. A verbal agreement to *deduct* cleaning costs from a bond does not legally bind you to *pay* an invoice later. While the agent may still pursue the cleaning cost as a separate debt if they believe you breached your tenancy agreement, they cannot force payment of an invoice simply because you verbally agreed to a bond deduction.

### What the Law Says About Cleaning & Bonds
* **Cleaning Costs from Bonds:** Under the Act, an agent is only entitled to claim the reasonable cost of cleaning from a bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean, taking into account fair wear and tear and the condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Professional Cleaning Rules:** The Regulations state that an agent cannot require professional cleaning unless it was carried out immediately before you moved in, or it is strictly necessary to restore the premises to their original condition based on the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
* **Claim Requirements:** Any claim for bond repayment must be made in a form approved by the RTBA and must specify the exact amount being refunded or apportioned [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

### What You Can Do
* **Do not feel pressured to pay the invoice immediately.** Since the bond was returned, the agent missed their statutory window to access those funds through the RTBA. 
* **Assess your obligation:** If you genuinely left the premises reasonably clean (considering fair wear and tear), you do not owe the money at all. You can politely decline the invoice and state that the tenancy has been concluded and the bond returned.
* **If you do owe the money but just didn't want it taken from the bond:** You are not legally forced to pay a retroactive invoice for a service you agreed to have deducted from a bond. If the agent insists, they would need to take you to VCAT to prove you owe the debt under your tenancy agreement. 
* **Keep records:** Save all emails, texts, and photos of the property's condition when you moved out. This protects you if the agent tries to dispute the matter later.

*Note: This information is based on Victorian residential tenancy law as it stands today. For personalised legal advice, you may contact VCAT or a community legal centre.*

**Short answer:** Under the current Act, the card fee is very likely not allowed, but the documents don't settle every point. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent doesn't change the answer, because the Act's main fee prohibition applies to "a person."

**Version relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026, also applies [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Fee-free method must be available:** The agent must ensure that a rent payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A bank transfer with no fee may meet this, but the documents don't define "reasonably available," so being slower may or may not matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost disclosure:** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees, before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Charges for electronic payment:** A person must not demand or receive a charge, or an indemnity for a charge, for the establishment or use of direct debit or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee for payment of rent:** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list the prescribed matters, so I can't confirm whether card fees fall within this.
- **Regulations:** The rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who receives the fee?

Not under the current text I could see. The charge prohibition applies to "a person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so it covers the app company as well as the agent. The earlier version of section 51A exempted providers and agents from the business-person fee rule [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but that version is no longer in force.

### What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent in writing which payment methods are available, and whether the card fee applies, before you choose a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to confirm that a fee-free method (such as bank transfer) is available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If the agent or app wants to pass the card fee to you, point out the charge prohibition in section 51(3)(b) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- What "prescribed matters" are under section 51A, so I can't confirm whether card fees are caught by that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- How "reasonably available" is interpreted, including whether a slower method counts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- How the disclosure duty in section 42(7) fits with the charge prohibition in section 51(3)(b). Section 42(7) refers to third-party fees a renter "may incur," which could be read as allowing some fees, but the documents don't resolve this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The complaint or enforcement process. Please check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisor before relying on this.

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents support a repair claim, and they point to a possible exit route. They do not contain a rent-reduction remedy.

## What the law says

- **Damp and mould are defined as urgent repairs.** The Act's definition includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises ... unsafe or insecure, including ... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It also includes "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The minimum standards are specific.** The premises must be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord must meet these standards before you move in.** The rental provider "must ensure that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and is vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in" and must "maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

**Repairs:**
- **Notify in writing.** Non-urgent damage must be notified "in writing, as soon as practicable" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs, the provider "must carry out urgent repairs after being notified" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Put your notice in writing.
- **Urgent repairs:** If you take reasonable steps to get the provider to act immediately and they don't, you may arrange the repairs. The provider may reimburse "the reasonable cost of repairs up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** The provider "must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time." You may apply to VCAT if they have not done the repairs "within 14 days of receiving notice" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does the work:** "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Cancelling:**
- The regulations refer to a renter giving notice to vacate "under section 91ZD of the Act on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation," and state that the provider is then not entitled to rent-foregone compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not contain the text of section 91ZD, so I cannot confirm the test for "unfit for habitation" or the notice steps. Get advice before relying on this.

**Lower rent:**
- The documents do not cover a rent reduction for disrepair. The only reduction mechanism I found is a VCAT order reducing the term of the agreement for severe hardship under section 91U [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That is not a rent cut, so I cannot say whether you can get lower rent.

## Your situation

You have not moved in, which matters for the move-in obligation above. The documents do not say how that affects your options beyond the points already covered.

## Sources

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026).

For the current rules and urgent repair list, see consumer.vic.gov.au/urgentrepairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This is general information, not legal advice. Consider speaking to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer before taking action.
