answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait indefinitely. Under the current Act, you may be able to arrange the urgent repair yourself, but only through a suitably qualified person, and you must follow the notice steps below. The documents don't say whether an owner's "only our tradespeople" rule changes this.

**What the law says**

- A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to immediately carry out the repairs, and they are unable to get the landlord or agent to do them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The regulations' sample agreement also gives "a burst water service" as an example of an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The full statutory definition is not in the documents I retrieved, so I can't confirm whether a whole-house water shut-off is covered.
- "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So doing it yourself, without a qualified person, is not what the law allows.
- The renter must give written notice of the damage or breakdown as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Put it in writing now.** Notice must be given as soon as practicable, and the sample agreement says the renter should notify the provider in writing for an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Send the email or letter to the owner and agent, not just phone calls, and keep records of your two calls.
2. **Arrange a suitably qualified person** (e.g., a licensed plumber) if the owner and agent still cannot get the repair done. The documents don't define "reasonable steps," so whether two calls today is enough is not something I can confirm.
3. **Give the provider 7 days' written notice** of the repairs and the cost after the work is done. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving that notice, up to the lesser of the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the cap:** the regulations say the provider may reimburse "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Costs above that amount are a problem.
5. **If the owner refuses to pay or you can't afford the repair,** you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out the urgent repairs. VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations also list these grounds: the renter cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Get help if needed:** Consumer Affairs Victoria is listed as 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether an owner can lawfully require you to use only their own tradespeople, and whether that overrides your right to arrange urgent repairs.
- What counts as "reasonable steps" in practice.
- Whether a whole-house water shut-off falls within the statutory definition of urgent repairs.

**Sources and versions**

- Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the current version in the documents.
- Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the owner keeps refusing, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT promptly.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if your DIY clean actually restored the carpets to their move-in condition. The law requires professional cleaning only where it is *required* to restore the premises, and the documents don't say who decides that or what evidence is needed.

**What the law says**

- A standard-form lease may include a term requiring professional cleaning only if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their pre-tenancy condition, taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed standard term says the provider must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy started and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- The renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, only "if professional cleaning becomes required" to restore the premises to that condition, again having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- A term requiring professional cleaning that isn't in the standard form is a prohibited term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the condition report.** The standard form ties the cleaning obligation to the condition report [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Compare the carpets with what that report recorded at the start. If it records them as clean, that supports your position.
2. **Ask the agent in writing what makes professional cleaning "required"**, and whether they are relying on paragraph (a) or (b) above. Ask them to identify the specific carpet problem that DIY cleaning did not fix.
3. **Keep evidence of the carpets' condition.** The documents don't list what evidence is acceptable. Dated photos, your cleaning receipts (for supplies or equipment), and any move-out inspection notes would help show the condition, but I can't confirm from these sources that they will be accepted.
4. **Seek the Tribunal's view if it stays disputed.** A renter may apply to the Tribunal to declare invalid or vary a term that is harsh or unconscionable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how the Tribunal would treat this particular dispute.

**Version and coverage notes**

- **Regulations:** The cleaning wording above comes from the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (metadata version "009", in force from 30 June 2026, with no end date listed) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force today. The same wording appeared in Authorised Version No. 002, which covered your 2024 start date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Act:** The section 27C text I cite comes from the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 110, which ran only until 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The latest Act version in my results (No. 111) ended on 29 June 2026, so I could not confirm the Act version in force today.
- **Pet clause:** The documents don't address pet clauses. The cleaning obligation is the relevant rule here, so check that your clause matches the standard-form wording.

**Which law applies:** The current version is Authorised Version No. 115 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (in force from 13 October 2026, the latest version retrieved) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its bond provisions are in Part 10, and I've relied on that version.

## What the law says about cleaning and bonds

- A landlord (called a "residential rental provider") can claim from the bond "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Bond claims are made to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority, and "a claim must be in a form approved by the Authority" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Before a landlord claims bond money for the renter to be repaid to the landlord, the landlord "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim" at least 3 days before the claim is made. That evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A landlord "must not request or obtain a renter's signature to a claim form" unless the form specifies the amount of bond to be refunded and any apportionment. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Your situation

- **Verbal or informal agreement to a deduction:** The documents set out a formal claim process, with an approved form and evidence. They don't say whether an informal agreement you gave, without signing a claim form, binds you to a deduction or to a later invoice. I can't determine that from these documents.
- **Invoice after the full bond was refunded:** The documents don't address whether a landlord can invoice a renter separately for cleaning after the bond has been returned in full. If the full bond came back, that suggests no cleaning claim was paid out of it, but the documents don't say what happened in your case.

## What you can ask or do

1. **Ask for the bond claim evidence.** Under the rules above, a landlord claiming cleaning costs from the bond must provide supporting evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Ask the agent for that evidence and for the condition report.
2. **Check the cleaning cost against the law.** The cost must be reasonable, and cleaning is claimable only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, judged against their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Consider the Tribunal.** A renter or other person with an interest in a bond claim may apply to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order. That application "must be made within 14 days after the residential rental agreement has terminated" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Given the timing you describe, check whether that window has already passed.
4. **Seek advice on the invoice.** The contents page of the Act lists sections on applications for loss or damage (s 213B) and compensation (s 209) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved material does not include the text of those sections, so I can't say how they apply to an invoice sent after bond refund. You may want advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy service.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether an informal or verbal agreement to a bond deduction is binding.
- Whether a landlord can issue a separate invoice for cleaning after returning the full bond.
- The full text of the Tribunal and compensation provisions (ss 209, 213B), which appear only in the table of contents.

## What the law says about your situation

- **Minimum standards.** The rented premises must be structurally sound and weatherproof. Each room must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Rotting timber isn't named in the excerpts. It may relate to structural soundness, but I can't confirm that from these documents.
- **The rental provider's duty at move-in.** Under the standard-form agreement, the rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. They must also be vacant and reasonably clean when you move in, and be kept in good repair and fit for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The Act's definition includes a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards. It also includes any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure, including mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs.** The documents support this.
- Notify the rental provider in writing. If the mould or damp is an urgent repair, the provider must carry it out after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may arrange urgent repairs yourself only if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't. You can then be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Record it in the condition report.** The prescribed condition report form says you should note anything unsafe or needing repair. Where the report lists something needing repair, that gives the provider written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You have 5 business days after moving in to complete it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you later find something wrong, you can apply to VCAT to correct the report within **30 days** after the start date of the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You haven't moved in, so take dated photos and send them to the provider with your written notice.

**3. Cancel the lease.** The retrieved documents don't answer this.
- The only reference is in the over-5-years form. It mentions a notice to vacate under section 91ZD "on the basis the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That is a form clause, not the operative section, so I can't say what it requires or whether it applies to you.
- The operative provisions of the Act on ending an agreement were not in the retrieved text, so I can't say whether you can cancel before moving in.

**4. Lower rent.** The retrieved documents don't answer this either. The rent provisions I found only deal with challenging a proposed rent increase as excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They don't cover a rent reduction for a defective property.

## Before you decide

You should check the operative sections of the Act on termination and rent reduction, or get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT. I wouldn't treat your lease as cancelled, or stop paying rent, until you have done that.

## What the law says

  - you are unable to get them to carry out the repairs.
- **Use a suitably qualified person, not a DIY fix.** The standard agreement terms say that only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner's "own tradespeople only" rule.** The documents I retrieved don't mention any right for the owner to limit which tradespeople do urgent repairs. The test in section 72(1) is whether you can get the rental provider or agent to carry out the repair [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a rental provider can lawfully restrict who does the work, so I can't say more on that.
- **Does your tap count as an "urgent repair"?** Section 3(1) defines urgent repairs, but I didn't retrieve that definition. The regulations' form refers to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and one form gives "a burst water service" as an example of an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these documents that a broken tap with the water off to the whole house qualifies, so check section 3(1).
- **Are two calls enough?** The Act doesn't define "reasonable steps" in the text I retrieved. Two unsuccessful calls today is a good start, but it is not confirmed to be enough.

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** The standard agreement says that if you need an urgent repair, you should notify the rental provider in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must also give written notice of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures as soon as practicable [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email counts as written notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **If they still don't act, arrange the repair yourself** through a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The regulations' form summary gives that amount as **$2500** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). **Practical tip:** keep a record of your calls (times and numbers), your written notice, and the tradesperson's invoice.

The renter's obligation to have premises professionally cleaned or to pay for it only arises if it becomes required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). ## What the law says

Today’s applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009, in force from 30 June 2026** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Because you have **not entered into possession**, section 91L applies. A residential rental agreement terminates if the renter gives the rental provider a notice of termination stating that the premises are, among other things, **not in good repair, unfit for human habitation, do not meet rental minimum standards, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The minimum standards require the premises to be **structurally sound and weatherproof**, and every room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Structural mould or damp is also defined as an **urgent repair**, as is a fault or damage making the premises unsafe or insecure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must provide and maintain the premises in **good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, regardless of whether the renter knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice terminating the agreement under section 91L.**  
   State that you have not entered into possession and that the damp, mould and rotting timber mean the premises are not in good repair and/or do not meet the rental minimum standards. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Ask for confirmation that the agreement is terminated and for return of any bond or rent paid; the retrieved documents do not specify the refund procedure or timing.

2. **Ask the rental provider to arrange repairs instead.**  
   Ask for suitably qualified tradespeople to investigate and repair the source of the damp, remove the mould safely, and replace or repair the rotting timber. Repairs required to discharge the provider’s repair duty must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The regulations also require each room to be free from structurally caused mould and damp and the premises to be structurally sound. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask to postpone occupation and rent until the work is complete.**  
   The provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the premises are not vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day, you are not required to enter occupation and are not required to pay rent for the period until you actually enter occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly state that rent is automatically suspended solely because of the mould, damp or timber defects before occupation.

4. **Ask for a lower rent, but do not reduce it unilaterally.**  
   The retrieved documents do not give a renter an automatic right to impose a lower rent because the premises are defective. You may ask the provider to agree in writing to a reduced rent, but the documents do not state that the provider must agree. A Tribunal compensation order, where available, may take the form of a rent refund or reduction. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

5. **If the provider disputes the problem or refuses to act, seek a Tribunal remedy.**  
   For non-urgent repairs, the Act permits an application for repair orders after written notice and 14 days without the repairs; the Tribunal may order specified repairs and compensation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) However, because you have not moved in, the clearest immediate statutory option on the facts given is the **section 91L termination notice**, rather than moving in and pursuing repairs.

Do not simply stop paying or walk away without giving written notice or obtaining written agreement, because the Act says a residential rental agreement can be terminated only in the ways provided by the Act or by agreement. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**What the Law Says**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, a broken tap that forces you to shut off your water supply qualifies as an **urgent repair** (specifically classified as a "burst water service" or failure of a water supply) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf). 

The current law states that if a renter has taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to carry out urgent repairs immediately, but is unable to get them to do so, the renter is legally permitted to arrange for those repairs themselves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). An owner's policy of only using their own tradespeople does not override this statutory right if those tradespeople are unavailable.

**What You Can Do Now**
You do not have to wait. Since you have already called twice today and they cannot attend immediately, you can proceed with the following steps:

1. **Hire a qualified professional:** Only a suitably qualified person may carry out urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 
2. **Keep detailed records:** Ensure you obtain a formal invoice/receipt itemising the work done and the cost.
3. **Notify the owner in writing:** Within 7 days of the repairs being completed, you must give the owner written notice detailing the repairs carried out and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
4. **Claim reimbursement:** The owner is legally liable to reimburse you for the reasonable cost of the repairs (up to a prescribed limit of $2,500) within 7 days of receiving your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). 

**If the Cost Exceeds $2,500 or You Cannot Pay Upfront**
If the repair costs more than $2,500, or if you cannot afford to pay for it yourself first, you do not have to arrange the repairs. Instead, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the owner (or their agent) to carry out the urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal is required to hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

*Note: This advice applies under the current Victorian residential tenancy laws in force today, specifically the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (v110)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (v002)**.*

The rules governing your lease are set out in Clause 12 of the standard form residential rental agreement, found in the ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*** (**Authorised Version rt-regs-2021-v005**), which is in force today [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 

According to this clause, a rental provider cannot require you to professionally clean the carpets at the end of your tenancy unless one of two specific conditions is met:
1. Professional cleaning was done immediately before you moved in **and** you were explicitly advised that it had been professionally cleaned; OR
2. Professional cleaning is actually required to restore the carpets to the same condition they were in when you started the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Since your carpets are back to their original state (minus normal wear and tear), the second condition does not apply, and the agent has no legal basis to demand a professional cleaning receipt.

**What Would Help Show the Carpets' Condition?**
To prove you have met your obligation, you should rely on the following:
* **The Signed Condition Report:** This is the primary legal benchmark for comparing the property's state at move-in versus move-out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Dated Photos or Videos:** Clear, timestamped photos or videos you took when you moved in and when you moved out will provide objective evidence that the carpets have not been damaged beyond fair wear and tear.
* **Written Correspondence:** If the agent continues to demand payment, reply in writing referencing Clause 12 of the standard form lease and attach your move-in/move-out photos alongside the signed condition report to demonstrate the carpets are in the required condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

No. 3/2021** (Version 009) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Here are your options before your fixed-term lease ends, based on this document:

### 1. Demand Urgent Repairs
Damaged plumbing and wiring likely constitute urgent repairs (such as a burst water service or failure of an essential service) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must notify your rental provider in writing immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The provider is responsible for ensuring these are fixed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If they fail to act, you may arrange for a suitably qualified person to do the work and claim reimbursement for reasonable costs up to $2,500, or apply to VCAT if the costs exceed this amount or you cannot afford them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Terminate the Agreement Early (Premises Unfit for Habitation)
Because the break-in caused significant damage that prevents you from living in or cleaning the property, you can give your rental provider notice of intention to vacate under section 91ZD of the Act on the basis that the premises are destroyed or unfit for habitation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
* **Key Benefit:** If you terminate under this ground, the rental provider **cannot** charge you compensation for "rent foregone" (the money they claim they will lose because you are leaving early) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 3. Apply to VCAT for Severe Hardship
Alternatively, if the situation causes you severe hardship due to unforeseen circumstances, you may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order to reduce the term of your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### 4. Document Everything Thoroughly
To ensure you are not held financially responsible for the burglary damage at the end of your tenancy, you must document everything. Take dated photos showing the condition of the premises and note the burglary-related damage on your condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The condition report is specifically designed to help resolve disputes over damage and cleaning, ensuring that fair wear and tear or third-party damage is not unfairly attributed to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

*Note: While the Regulations provide these standard terms, they reference specific sections of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (such as section 91ZD). **1. Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?**
No, they are legally distinct processes. Under Victorian law, a bond deduction is a formal statutory claim that must be submitted using a specific form approved by the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because you never signed this required claim form and your full bond was returned to you, no valid bond claim was ever processed against your money [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Verbally agreeing that an agent *could* take money from the bond does not constitute signing the statutory form.

**2. Do you have to pay the separate invoice?**
The Act regulates how bonds are held and claimed, but it does not automatically validate or invalidate private invoices sent after a tenancy ends [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Bond Claim Rules:** A residential rental provider is only entitled to claim cleaning costs from a bond if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, taking into account fair wear and tear and the initial condition of the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since your bond was returned in full without a signed claim form, the agent cannot retroactively deduct money from the bond.
*   **The Invoice:** Whether you must pay the separate invoice depends on your specific lease agreement and whether the cleaning was actually required under those terms. However, because the tenancy has ended and the bond was fully refunded, the agent cannot force payment through the bond system. 

**What you can do:**
*   **Do not sign anything new** acknowledging the debt unless you agree with the amount and the work was genuinely required.
*   **Request evidence** of the property's condition at move-out versus move-in to verify if professional cleaning or restoration was actually necessary under the lease terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   If the agent continues to demand payment, you can seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or consider disputing the invoice through small claims processes if it is unreasonable.
